The reframe

## An address is not
the hard part any more.

If you are searching for an LMS with a custom domain, you have already decided the important thing — that your students should arrive at your name, not somebody else's platform address — and the only question left is how much difficulty and money that decision costs. In 2026 the honest answer is: almost none of either. The connection is two DNS records, the certificate issues itself, and the site is live in minutes. The difficulty educators still describe when they talk about getting a website is a memory of a different decade.

That memory is worth naming, because it is what stops people. For most of the last ten years, an Indian educator who wanted a course website on their own domain was quoted somewhere between ₹40,000 and ₹2 lakh, told it would take four to eight weeks, and handed a WordPress installation with eleven plugins that would need maintaining forever. The quote was not dishonest — that genuinely was the work. But it created a belief that owning your address is an advanced, expensive, late-stage move. It is not. It is now the cheapest part of the exercise.

So this guide reframes the question. Not how do I get a website on my own domain — that is solved, and the mechanics take one section to explain. The real questions are: what has to work behind that address before it is worth sending a paying student to it; which providers give you those things and at what price; and what an owned address actually buys you, as opposed to what educators hope it buys them. The last one is where most of the disappointment lives, and it is the one nobody selling you a website will raise.

Across the educators we work with, the pattern is consistent: the domain is never the reason a coaching site fails. It fails because there was nothing behind the address worth paying for, or because nobody knew the address existed.

One clarification before the mechanics, because it decides how you read everything below. A learning management system and a website builder solve different problems that look identical from outside. A website builder produces pages. An LMS produces enrolments, entitlements and results — it knows which student paid for which batch, which lecture they may open, what they scored, and what happens when their access expires. You can build a handsome coaching website on a page builder and still have no way to stop a ₹12,000 course being forwarded to a WhatsApp group of two hundred. That distinction is the whole subject of the nine layers.

· · ·

The shift

## What actually changed —
the LMS became the website.

The change that made this easy was architectural, not cosmetic. Course platforms used to be a walled application you sent students into — a login page with a vendor's name on it, hanging off the side of a marketing website you maintained separately. The marketing site was yours; the classroom was theirs; the two were joined by a link and a prayer. Educators paid twice, maintained two systems, and lost students in the gap between them.

What replaced it is a single system that renders both the public storefront and the private classroom under one address. The pages a prospective student browses — your subjects, your batches, your fees, your credentials — and the pages a paid student opens — the lecture, the PDF, the mock test, the score — are the same application, differing only by who is logged in. Once that is true, the domain stops being a website-shaped problem and becomes a routing problem, which is a problem computers solved in the 1980s.

Three things had to arrive together for this to work at Indian price points, and they did. Free automated certificates removed the last recurring cost and the last manual step from HTTPS. Edge routing that can serve thousands of separate domains from shared infrastructure made per-educator custom domains cheap to operate rather than a bespoke deployment each time. And UPI made checkout on an individual educator's site feel as safe to an Indian student as checkout on a large marketplace — a trust problem, not a technical one, and arguably the hardest of the three.

Reframe

### You are not buying a website. You are choosing where your students' records live.

The address is a five-minute decision. The system behind it holds every enrolment, every payment, every test score and every phone number you will ever collect — and the cost of moving that later is the only lock-in that has ever mattered.

This is also why "get a website made" has become bad advice for most educators. A brochure site built by a freelancer for ₹25,000 will look good and do nothing: it cannot take a payment, gate a lecture, score a test, or tell you who watched what. Six months later you buy an LMS anyway, and the brochure becomes a second thing to maintain. If you are weighing that fork, the longer argument is in running an online coaching academy without coding, and the page-level craft is in how to create a landing page for an online course.

· · ·

The anatomy

## The nine layers behind
a working coaching site.

A coaching website that actually earns money is nine systems wearing one address. Educators comparing providers almost always compare layer one and layer nine — how the homepage looks, and whether support answers — because those are the only two visible from the outside. The seven in between are where the money leaks. Listing them in order is the single most useful thing you can do before reading any vendor's pricing page, because it converts a feature list into a checklist you can hold each of them to.

LayerWhat it must doWhat breaks without itUsually supplied by
1 · Address & routingServe your academy at a domain you own, over HTTPS, with certificates that renew themselvesExpired certificate takes the whole paid site down at oncePlatform, once you add two DNS records
2 · StorefrontExplain who you teach, for which exam, at what fee, with proof — and convertTraffic arrives and leaves; no enquiriesTemplates in the platform
3 · CatalogueHold courses, batches, note sets and test series as separately priced, separately dated itemsEverything becomes one blob you cannot price or scheduleThe LMS
4 · EntitlementsKnow exactly which student may open which item, until whenOne paid login circulates; revenue quietly collapsesThe LMS — never a page builder
5 · DeliveryStream lectures on a ₹200 data pack and open PDFs without a download linkBuffering complaints, refunds, forwarded filesPlatform CDN, or a paid video host
6 · AssessmentRun timed tests, auto-score, rank, and show a solution the student learns fromYou return to sharing PDFs on WhatsApp and marking by handThe LMS test engine
7 · MoneyTake UPI, cards and net banking, issue a receipt, settle to your bank on a known cycleCollection becomes a personal UPI ID and a spreadsheetPlatform-integrated gateway
8 · RecordsKeep student, payment and progress history in one exportable placeYou cannot answer a parent, a dispute, or your own accountantStudent CRM inside the platform
9 · RecoveryBackups, uptime, and a human who answers when a batch of 200 cannot log inA Sunday outage becomes a refund eventWhoever you are paying — check this before you pay

Read layer four twice. Entitlement is the layer educators skip and the one that decides whether the business survives contact with real students. A page builder with a payment button gives you layers one, two and seven and nothing else — which is why so many ₹25,000 coaching websites end with lectures on an unlisted YouTube playlist and a Drive folder whose link is now in three WhatsApp groups. The related economics are laid out in the best platform for selling PDF notes and test series.

Question Often Asked

### Can I just use a website builder plus Google Drive instead of an LMS?

You can, and for a first ₹500 note set it is a reasonable way to test demand without spending anything. It stops working the moment the price rises or the batch grows. A Drive link has no concept of who paid, no expiry, no per-student access, and no way to revoke — so the first student who shares it has effectively made your product free, and you will not know it happened. The practical threshold is around the point where a single item costs more than ₹1,000 or a batch crosses about thirty students. Past that, you are not saving money by avoiding an LMS; you are financing your own leakage.

· · ·

The mechanics

## How connecting your own domain
really works.

Connecting a custom domain to an LMS is a directory update, not a migration. Nothing is uploaded, nothing is copied, and no files move. You are editing the internet's phone book so that requests for yourinstitute.com are answered by the servers already running your academy. That is why it takes minutes rather than weeks, and why it can be undone just as fast if you change your mind.

Two records do all of it, and it is worth understanding what each one is for rather than pasting them blind.

1Record one

### A TXT record that proves the domain is yours

The platform generates a short unique string and asks you to publish it in your domain's DNS. Only someone with access to the registrar account can do that, so seeing the string is proof of control. It stops anyone from claiming a domain they do not own — including importantly, someone claiming yours.

2Record two

### A CNAME record that points the domain at the platform

This is the record that actually routes students. It makes your name an alias for the platform's address, so every request for your site is answered by the infrastructure serving your academy. On the bare apex form of a domain some registrars need an A record or an ALIAS-style record instead — a DNS standards quirk, not a platform limitation.

After that, the work is automatic. The platform re-checks DNS every few minutes; the moment both records resolve, it enables the domain and requests the HTTPS certificate itself, then renews it on its own schedule from then on. You are never asked to buy, install or remember a certificate. In practice this whole sequence finishes in minutes.

Why automatic renewal stopped being optional in 2026. Certificate lifetimes are collapsing across the industry, and Let's Encrypt — which underpins a very large share of the web's free HTTPS — switched its main issuance profile to 45-day certificates in May 2026, down from 90[1]. A stack that requires a human to renew now requires that human eight times a year, forever. Miss once and every student sees a browser security warning instead of your class.

Two practical details save most of the support tickets. First, enter the domain without the https prefix and without a trailing slash — the field wants the name, not the URL. Second, lower the TTL on your DNS records to around 300 seconds before you make the change. TTL is how long other networks are allowed to cache the old answer; leaving it at a default of 24 hours is the single most common reason a correctly configured domain appears not to work yet.

Question Often Asked

### How long does a custom domain actually take to go live?

Usually a few minutes, and the delay is almost never the platform. Verification and certificate issuance are automatic once both records resolve. What varies is DNS propagation — the time for your change to reach every network — which is typically under an hour and can stretch to 24 to 48 hours in the worst case, depending on the TTL that was in place before you edited and how aggressively intermediate resolvers cache. If nothing has happened after an hour, the cause is almost always a typo in the pasted record, a record added to the wrong domain, or a registrar that silently appends the domain name to the host field, producing yourinstitute.com.yourinstitute.com.

One more thing worth knowing before you start: on AllCoaching your free address keeps working. Every academy is published at yourname.allcoaching.in the moment it is created, and that address continues to resolve after the custom domain is connected. Every link you already sent — the WhatsApp forward, the Telegram post, the number printed on a pamphlet — keeps working instead of quietly becoming a dead end the day you upgrade.

· · ·

The sequencing

## Free subdomain vs your own domain —
when each is right.

A free subdomain and a custom domain are not a cheap option and a good option. They are the right answer at two different moments, and the cost of getting the order wrong is larger than the cost of the domain. The subdomain's job is to let you find out whether anyone will pay. The custom domain's job is to make sure the reputation you then build accrues to you.

The common sequence

Buy a domain. Wait for a site to be built. Argue about the logo. Discover in week six that the fee page is wrong. Launch to nobody. Conclude that online teaching does not work.

The sequence that works

Publish on the free address the same day. Sell one batch. Learn what students actually ask before paying. Then buy the domain, connect it in minutes, and point everything at a page you already know converts.

The argument for starting free is not thrift, it is information. The first version of your fee structure, your batch names and your course description is almost always wrong, and you find out by selling, not by planning. An address you can publish in an afternoon lets you be wrong cheaply. An address that arrives at the end of a six-week build makes being wrong expensive enough that most educators defend the mistake instead of fixing it.

The argument for moving to your own domain is equally concrete, and it is about accrual. Everything the site earns — search rankings, backlinks, the pamphlets in circulation, the number students have saved, the mentions that AI assistants read when deciding who to recommend — attaches to whatever address it appeared at. On a platform subdomain, part of that value is attached to an address you do not control. On your own domain, all of it is yours, and it survives any decision you later make about providers. Move once, early, before there is much to move.

Question Often Asked

### Do I need to buy a domain before I can start selling courses online in India?

No, and buying one first is a common way to lose two weeks. On AllCoaching every academy is published at a free yourname.allcoaching.in address from the moment it is created, and that page can take a real UPI payment the same day — no monthly fee to reach that point. Students in India routinely pay on platform subdomains; what they check before paying is whether the page loads over HTTPS, whether the fee and syllabus are stated plainly, and whether the teacher looks real. Buy the domain once there is something on the page worth visiting. The domain itself costs ₹600 to ₹1,200 a year at your registrar, connecting it to AllCoaching is included in every plan, from ₹6,999 a year, and it goes live in minutes whenever you are ready.

There is one case where the order reverses: if you already have a domain — an old brochure site, a name you registered years ago, a printed address on hoardings and pamphlets — connect it immediately. You are not buying anything, the recognition already exists, and every week the old address points at a dead brochure is a week of wasted attention. If that old site currently ranks for anything, read the section on moving without losing rankings before you switch it over.

The landscape

## What each kind of provider
actually gives you.

Everything sold to Indian educators as "a website for your coaching" falls into five categories, and they differ far more in what they leave you holding than in what they show on the pricing page. The useful question is never which is best — it is which layers from the list of nine each one supplies, and which it quietly leaves as your problem.

Two honest readings of that table. First, a custom domain is not an expensive feature — it is a fence. The economics

## The real ₹ math of getting live
on your own domain.

Here is the Year-1 arithmetic for an Indian educator who wants a full LMS answering at a domain they own, laid out by route. Ranges rather than single numbers, because the honest spread is wide and anyone quoting you one number is quoting their own situation, not yours.

₹6,999Due before your first sale on a free platform address
₹600–1,200A year — what the domain itself actually costs at a registrar
2DNS records that perform the entire connection

Route A · Self-hosted WordPress and an LMS plugin

### ₹55,000 – ₹2,75,000 in Year 1, every rupee of it before your first sale

Domain ₹600–1,200. Hosting that will not fall over during a live batch ₹6,000–36,000. LMS licence ₹22,000–53,000. Video hosting and bandwidth ₹6,000–60,000. Theme, page builder and add-ons ₹5,000–25,000. Someone to set it up and keep it patched ₹15,000–1,00,000. You own everything and you maintain everything — including on the Sunday morning a plugin update breaks checkout during an admission window.

Route B · Global course platforms

### ₹55,000 – ₹2,06,000 a year, billed in a currency you do not earn in

The entry tier that includes a custom domain runs from roughly ₹4,600 a month at the cheapest to over ₹16,000 a month where the domain sits on a higher tier. Add the registrar bill. The real cost is not the number, it is the currency — your subscription is set in dollars while your fees are collected in rupees, so a bad quarter for the rupee raises your costs without anyone telling you.

Route C · Indian LMS and app SaaS

### ₹20,000 – ₹1,08,000 a year, plus whatever the contract adds

Published Indian plans start around ₹3,499 a month and rise steeply once you want platform branding removed; listed annual plans elsewhere in this bracket run ₹19,999 to ₹31,999. Ask three questions before signing: is there a setup fee, is there a share of sales on top of the subscription, and what is the renewal escalation. All three are common and none of them lead the pricing page.

Route D · Marketplace-backed studio

### ₹6,999 a year to be live and selling on your own name — after a 7-day free trial

Getting started costs ₹6,999 a year on Starter — the full LMS, your own domain, checkout, payouts, CRM and marketplace listing are included in every plan, with a 10% platform fee on Starter only on what you actually sell, or 0% commission on Growth (₹7,999 a month) and Pro (₹14,999 a month). Running on your own domain is included in every plan, with courses, tests, notes, logins and an installable phone app all included, plus the ₹600–1,200 a year you pay your own registrar. Compare that against ₹55,000–₹2,06,000 every year in Route B and the shape of the difference is not the number, it is the recurrence.

### What every plan actually covers

One thing worth stating plainly, because burying it would be the dishonest move: every plan covers the whole academy. Starter at ₹6,999 a year, Growth at ₹7,999 a month and Pro at ₹14,999 a month all cover the studio, your academy website, the student app on your own domain, recorded courses, PDF notes, test series, live classes, checkout, payouts and the marketplace listing. There is no per-hour meter on live video and no tier that unlocks the custom domain later; Growth and Pro add more video storage and streaming, and Pro adds the iOS app.

On Starter, the only other money that moves is a share of what you actually sell — a 10% platform fee, so you keep 90%. On Growth and Pro the commission is 0%, so you keep 100% of every sale, settled to your bank automatically. That is the whole commercial model, and it fits in two sentences, which is not something most platforms in this category can say.

Question Often Asked

### So what do I actually pay to run a full coaching business on my own domain?

Three separate things, and only one of them is unavoidable. Getting started is Starter at ₹6,999 a year — listing on the marketplace, onboarding your institute, hosting recorded courses, notes and test series, taking payments and getting paid out are included, with a 10% platform fee taken only from completed sales, so you keep 90%. Growth (₹7,999 a month) and Pro (₹14,999 a month) charge 0% commission, so you keep 100%. Your own domain is included in every plan, from ₹6,999 a year, which puts the full student app on that address — courses, tests, notes, logins and an installable phone app —. Live classes are included in every plan, with no separate live-class fee. On Starter, beyond the yearly fee, an educator selling recorded material pays nothing more until a sale happens.

Now the comparison people skip. Route A is not cheaper because it is self-hosted, and Route D is not cheaper at every revenue level. A route with a fixed annual cost gets relatively cheaper as you grow; a route that takes a percentage gets relatively more expensive. On AllCoaching's own plans (illustrative, before GST): at ₹4 lakh of annual sales, Starter costs ₹6,999 plus ₹40,000 in fees, about ₹47,000, while Growth paid yearly is ₹79,990. At ₹25 lakh, Starter would cost about ₹2.57 lakh, and Growth at ₹79,990 with 0% commission is far lower. Do that arithmetic at your own realistic number, at year one and again at year three, before you let anyone — including this article — tell you what is cheapest.

In our experience watching educators make this decision through 2026, the mistake is almost never picking the wrong route. It is picking any route before knowing whether the teaching sells at all — committing ₹1.5 lakh to infrastructure for a batch that had not yet been proven to exist. The route with the smallest fixed cost before the first sale is not the best route for everyone forever. It is the only sane route for the period in which you do not yet know. Pricing judgement more broadly is covered in how to price online courses in India.

· · ·

The invisible layer

## The security you cannot see
from the address bar.

A padlock in the address bar tells a student exactly one thing: that the connection between their phone and the server is encrypted. It says nothing about whether the lecture behind it can be downloaded, whether the PDF link works for someone who never paid, whether your student list is exportable by you, or whether anyone would notice if it were exported by someone else. HTTPS is the floor, not the building — and on a site collecting fees and minors' details, the difference matters legally as well as commercially.

Six questions separate a secure setup from a decorated one. Ask them of any provider, including us, and treat a vague answer as an answer.

1Transport

### Is the certificate issued and renewed without me?

With certificate lifetimes now as short as 45 days[1], any arrangement where a human remembers to renew is a scheduled outage. The correct answer is that the platform issues and renews it automatically and you never see it.

2Entitlement

### Is access bound to a logged-in student, or to a link?

This is the difference between a business and a leak. If a lecture or note set opens for anyone holding the URL, you are not selling access — you are selling the first copy. Access should resolve against the student account that paid, and end when their entitlement does.

3Delivery

### Are video and PDF served through the platform, or from a public folder?

Content on an unlisted YouTube link or an open Drive folder is public content with an obscure address. Serving through the platform means the file is fetched for an authenticated session rather than handed over permanently. Deeper treatment sits in secure video hosting for educational content.

4Money

### Do card details ever touch anything I control?

They should not, ever. Checkout should be handled by a regulated gateway so that card data never reaches your site, your laptop or your WhatsApp. This is also why collecting fees on a personal UPI ID stops being viable the moment you need receipts, refunds and a record — see the best UPI payment gateway for online courses.

5Student data

### Can I export everything, and can a student have their data deleted?

Both matter. Export is your exit route; deletion is an obligation under the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, and your students are frequently minors. A provider who cannot demonstrate either is asking you to carry a legal risk on their behalf. Context in Indian EdTech laws and regulations for teachers.

6Recovery

### Who answers on a Sunday when 200 students cannot log in?

Backups, uptime and a reachable human are a security property, because an outage during an admission window costs the same as a breach and happens far more often. Ask what the support channel is and what the response window is before you need it.

Be precise about what any platform actually promises. Encrypted delivery, gated access and platform-served files are ordinary hygiene. Hard anti-piracy — device-locked playback, forensic watermarking, licensed DRM — is a separate and heavier layer, and any vendor implying the first is the second is telling you something that will be tested by your first popular course. The realistic version of that argument is in video DRM protection for Indian course creators and protecting course content from piracy for free.

On AllCoaching, the parts of that list the platform is responsible for are structural rather than optional: the HTTPS certificate on your custom domain is issued and renewed by the platform, content is served to authenticated students rather than as open links, checkout runs through the platform's payment rails so card data never reaches you, and student and payment records live in your studio in exportable form. What we do not claim is a hard DRM layer, because claiming it would be the kind of thing you only discover was untrue after it mattered.

· · ·

The compounding asset

## Why an owned domain compounds —
in Google and in AI answers.

An owned domain is the only part of an educator's online presence that appreciates. Rankings, links, citations, saved bookmarks, printed pamphlets, the address a former student gives a junior — all of it attaches to whatever name it appeared under. On a platform address, part of that accrual belongs to the platform. On your own domain, all of it is yours, and it survives every future decision you make about software. That is the entire case for a custom domain, and it is enough on its own.

What has changed since 2024 is where the accrual pays off. Students increasingly ask an assistant rather than a search box — who is the best UPSC economy teacher in Hindi, where can I buy a CAT quant test series — and the systems answering those questions decide who to name by assembling an entity from consistent mentions across the web. A single stable domain that carries your name, your subjects, your faculty page and your fees is a far cleaner entity to assemble than a scatter of platform profiles. This is the practical reason a domain now matters more than it did, and the mechanics are covered in SEO strategies for online course creators.

Question Often Asked

### Will moving from a platform subdomain to my own domain hurt my Google rankings?

Not if the move is done the way Google itself documents. Its site-move guidance is to redirect every old URL to its exact new equivalent, keep those redirects in place for as long as possible and at minimum a year, and submit a Change of Address in Search Console for every verified variant of the old address, including www and non-www forms[8]. Done that way, ranking signals transfer rather than reset. There is a rankings dip in the weeks around any move, which is precisely why moving early — while the old address has little accumulated authority to lose — is the cheapest possible time to do it. Waiting three years to buy a domain does not avoid the cost; it just makes it larger.

Two mistakes waste an owned domain more reliably than anything Google does. The first is running the same content at two addresses at once — an old brochure site and a new academy, both live, both indexed, competing with each other. Pick one, redirect the other. The second is treating the domain as the marketing plan. A domain is a place for attention to land. It does not create attention, and no amount of technical polish converts a page nobody has reached.

· · ·

The playbook

## The 7-step launch —
registrar to first sale.

This is the full sequence, in the order that wastes the least money. Steps three to five are the domain connection itself and take minutes. Steps one, six and seven are the ones educators skip, and they are the ones that decide whether the site earns. If you would rather see the studio before doing any of this, the live demo opens with no sign-up and every button works.

1Step 01

### Publish on the free subdomain first

Every academy gets a free address of the form yourname.allcoaching.in the moment it is created, with nothing to configure. Publish there and sell from it. A domain purchase is worth making once there is something on the page worth visiting, not before.

2Step 02

### Buy the domain in your own name

Register it yourself at GoDaddy, Namecheap, Hostinger or any registrar for roughly ₹600–1,200 a year. Use your own email and your own payment method, keep auto-renew on, and never let an agency or a relative hold the account. Whoever controls the registrar login controls the address — not whoever paid for it.

3Step 03

### Enter the domain in your studio, without the https prefix

Open the website settings and type the domain exactly as you own it — no https, no trailing slash. The platform generates the two records. Connecting your own domain is included in every plan, from ₹6,999 a year, so settle that first — the plan fee is all you pay to start whether or not you ever connect one.

4Step 04

### Paste the TXT and CNAME records at your registrar

Open the DNS panel and add both records exactly as shown. Copy and paste rather than retyping, and set a low TTL such as 300 seconds. If your registrar appends the domain name to the host field automatically, watch for the doubled-name mistake — it is the most common failure of the whole process.

5Step 05

### Let verification and HTTPS complete by themselves

The platform re-checks every few minutes, turns the domain on once both records resolve, and issues the certificate automatically — renewing it on its own from then on. Usually minutes; DNS can take up to 24–48 hours to reach every network in the worst case. Your free address keeps working throughout.

6Step 06

### Load real content before you announce the address

At minimum: one complete course, one PDF note set and one test series behind the checkout, plus a template, a logo and a plain paragraph saying who you teach and for which exam. A live domain with an empty catalogue converts nothing, and a first impression on a paid site is expensive to repair.

7Step 07

### Run one real purchase end to end before telling anyone

Buy one of your own items for a small amount, from a phone not logged in as the educator. Confirm the payment completes, the receipt arrives, access unlocks immediately, the video and PDF open, and the sale appears in your studio with the payout recorded. Only then send the link to students.

Realistic timeline. Steps 3 to 5 — the actual domain connection — take minutes. Step 2 depends on how long you take to choose a name. Step 6 is the real project, and for most educators it is a weekend. Total elapsed time for someone with content ready: one to two days, of which the technical portion is under ten minutes.

· · ·

The failure modes

## Six mistakes that make
a beautiful site earn nothing.

None of these are technical failures. Every one of them is a decision made early, for a sensible-sounding reason, that becomes expensive later. They are listed in the order they usually happen.

Mistake 01

### Letting someone else register the domain

The agency does it, or a cousin who is good with computers, and the account sits under their email with their card on file. Two years later the relationship ends or the card expires, and the address your entire student base knows is controlled by someone who no longer answers your calls. Register it yourself, keep auto-renew on, and store the login where you can find it.

Mistake 02

### Buying the domain before the content exists

The domain becomes the project. Weeks go into a logo and a colour, and no batch is sold. The purchase feels like progress precisely because it is the only step that can be completed without teaching anything. Publish free, sell one batch, then buy the name.

Mistake 03

### Choosing a name that borrows someone else's

A near-copy of a large institute's name looks like a shortcut to credibility and is a liability with a delay fuse. It invites a legal notice, it confuses the students you do reach, and it makes you permanently unrankable against the brand you imitated. An ordinary name you own outright beats a clever name you are borrowing.

Mistake 04

### Launching an empty catalogue

The domain resolves, the design is good, and there is one course listed as "coming soon". Every visitor you spent effort attracting arrives, finds nothing purchasable, and does not come back. Attention is the scarcest thing you have and it does not queue. Do not announce until at least one complete item can be bought.

Mistake 05

### Assuming the domain brings traffic

This is the expensive one. A new domain has no visitors, no rankings and no history — it is a shop on a street nobody walks down yet. Educators consistently expect a measurable lift on the day they switch addresses, and there is none. The domain changes who owns the door, not how many people walk through it.

Mistake 06

### Never running a real test purchase

The first person to discover the checkout is broken should not be a paying student. Buy your own item at a small price from a logged-out phone and follow it through to the payout record. Ten minutes here prevents the specific failure that costs both the sale and the reputation.

· · ·

The honest limit

## The part a website
will never solve.

Everything above is true and none of it produces a student. A domain, an LMS, a certificate, a template and a checkout together give you a shop that works perfectly. What they do not give you is anyone walking past it. This is the constraint that survives every technology decision an educator makes, and it is the reason so many well-built coaching sites sit at a handful of visits a month while their owners conclude that online teaching does not work.

The reason is structural rather than personal. A standalone website has no network effect. Every visitor must be brought to it individually, by you, at your cost — a reel, an ad, a WhatsApp forward, a hoarding. Nothing about another educator succeeding makes your site easier to find, and nothing about your hundredth student makes your hundred-and-first cheaper to acquire. The cost of attention rises with competition and never falls with scale, which is precisely backwards from how a business should behave.

"Content is king, but distribution is queen and she wears the pants."

— Jonathan Perelman, formerly of BuzzFeed

A marketplace inverts that arithmetic, and it is the only structure that does. When students arrive to browse rather than to visit one known name, every educator on the platform is discoverable by people who did not come looking for them — and each additional educator makes the destination more worth visiting, which makes discovery cheaper for everyone already there. That is a compounding asset; an advertising budget is a consumable. This is why AllCoaching pairs the branded academy on your own domain with a shared student marketplace instead of selling only the software: the domain answers who owns this, and the marketplace answers how does anyone find it.

It is worth being exact about what this does and does not mean, because overpromising here is the standard industry move. A marketplace listing is not a guarantee of students, and it does not make a weak course sell. What it changes is the source of attention: instead of every visitor being one you paid for, some fraction arrives because the destination itself has traffic. For an educator with no existing audience that fraction is the entire difference between a live site and a business. The longer form of this argument sits in the EdTech marketplace answer to app fatigue in India and the four real alternatives to a personal coaching app.

The test

### Ask any provider: where does my first visitor come from?

If the answer is a variant of "you bring them", you are buying a container. That may be exactly what you need — but price it accordingly, and add the acquisition budget to the quote before comparing it with anything else.

· · ·

The verdict

## The verdict.

So: an LMS on your own custom domain, in 2026, is two DNS records and a few minutes, and it costs ₹600–1,200 a year for the domain plus whatever your provider charges to point at it. The technical difficulty that kept Indian educators renting somebody else's address for a decade is gone. If you already own a domain, connect it this week — there is no argument for leaving it pointed at a dead brochure. If you do not, publish on a free address today, sell one batch, and buy the name once you know what it should say.

What has not changed is the harder half. The nine layers behind the address still have to work — particularly entitlement, delivery and money, which is where page builders quietly fail and where the difference between an LMS and a website becomes a revenue number rather than a preference. And no configuration of any of it produces a student. A domain decides who owns the door. It does not decide how many people walk through it. Any provider who lets you believe otherwise is selling you a container and calling it a business.

Across the educators we have watched launch through 2026, the ones who do this well share a short discipline:

- They sell before they build — one batch on a free address beats six weeks of design.

- They register the domain themselves — own email, own card, auto-renew on, no exceptions.

- They check entitlement before aesthetics — who can open what, until when, is the layer that pays.

- They run one real test purchase — logged out, on a phone, all the way to the payout record.

- They budget for attention, not just software — or they choose a model that supplies some of it.

- They compute cost at their own revenue — at year one and again at year three, not in the abstract.

Do that and the decision stops being frightening. It becomes what it actually is: a cheap, reversible, ten-minute technical step, wrapped around the only question that ever mattered — whether enough people know your teaching exists. Figures for other platforms in this guide were read from their own public pricing pages in September 2026 and are ranges, not quotes; verify directly before deciding.

"Every educator who asked me how to get a website on their own domain was really asking a question about permanence — whether the thing they were building would still be theirs in five years. The address was never the answer to that. Who holds the records was."

— Amit Ratan, Founder & CEO, AllCoaching

Glossary

## Glossary —
key terms.

Term

### Custom Domain

A web address you register and control yourself, such as yourinstitute.com, pointed at a platform that serves your academy. Distinct from a branded theme: branding changes what the page looks like, a custom domain changes who owns the address the page lives at.

Term

### Subdomain

An address issued under a parent domain, such as yourname.allcoaching.in. It is free, instant and fully functional for selling, but the parent domain belongs to the platform, so the address itself is borrowed rather than owned.

Term

### DNS

The Domain Name System, the internet's directory that translates a human-readable name into the server that answers for it. Connecting a domain to a platform is entirely a DNS exercise; no files move anywhere.

Term

### CNAME Record

A DNS entry that makes one name an alias for another, so requests for your domain are answered by the platform's servers. It is the record that actually routes your students, and it works on subdomains such as www but not on every apex domain.

Term

### TXT Verification Record

A short string the platform asks you to publish in your domain's DNS to prove you control it. It exists so nobody can claim a domain they do not own; once seen by the platform it has done its job and simply stays in place.

Term

### Apex Domain

The bare form of a domain with no prefix, such as example.com rather than www.example.com. It matters in practice because the DNS standard restricts CNAME records at the apex, which is why some registrars require an A record or an ALIAS-style record there instead.

Term

### TLS Certificate

The credential that turns http into https and puts the padlock in the address bar. Modern certificates are short-lived and issued automatically, which makes automatic renewal a requirement rather than a convenience: an unrenewed certificate takes a paid course site offline for every student at once.

Term

### DNS Propagation

The delay between changing a DNS record and every network worldwide seeing the change, caused by caching at intermediate resolvers. Lowering the TTL before a change shortens it; it is the single most common reason a correctly configured domain appears not to work yet.

Term

### Learning Management System

Software that hosts courses, delivers video and notes, runs assessments, tracks progress and controls who can access what. Distinct from a website builder, which produces pages: an LMS produces enrolments, entitlements and results.

Term

### White-Label Academy

A platform-run academy presented entirely under the educator's own name, logo and domain, with the vendor invisible to students. It removes the vendor's branding but not the vendor's role, which is why data export and exit terms matter more than the logo does.

FAQ

## Frequently asked
questions.

What is an LMS with a custom domain?
It is a learning management system — course hosting, video, notes, test series, student logins and checkout — served to your students at a web address you own, such as yourinstitute.com, instead of a platform address. The software still runs on the provider's infrastructure. What changes is the name on the door: students see only your brand, links you share carry your name, and the search authority the site earns accumulates against an address that stays yours if you ever move providers.

Do I need my own domain to start selling courses online in India?
No, and buying one first is a common way to waste two weeks. On AllCoaching every academy is published at a free address of the form yourname.allcoaching.in from the moment it is created, and that page can take real payments the same day. A domain is worth buying once there is something on the page worth visiting. Sell first, then upgrade the address.

How do I connect my own domain to my coaching website?
Two DNS records do the whole job. You type your domain into the studio without the https prefix, and the platform generates a TXT record that proves the domain is yours and a CNAME record that points it at the platform. You paste both into the DNS panel at your registrar — GoDaddy, Namecheap, Hostinger or whoever you bought from. The platform re-checks every few minutes, turns the domain on by itself, and issues the HTTPS certificate automatically.

How long does it take for a custom domain to go live?
Usually a few minutes. Once both DNS records resolve, verification and certificate issuance complete without anyone touching anything. The variable is not the platform but DNS itself: changes can take up to 24 to 48 hours to reach every network in the worst case, and some registrars cache aggressively. Setting a low TTL, such as 300 seconds, before you make the change shortens that tail considerably.

Does AllCoaching sell domains?
No. You buy the domain yourself from any registrar and connect it, which is deliberate. A domain registered in your own account, with your own email and payment method, is one of the few genuinely portable assets an educator owns. If the platform held the registration, leaving would mean leaving the address behind — and that is exactly the dependency this feature exists to remove.

Does my free allcoaching.in address stop working after I connect my own domain?
No. Both keep working. The free yourname.allcoaching.in address continues to resolve alongside the custom domain, which matters more than it sounds: every WhatsApp forward, Telegram post and printed poster carrying the old link keeps working, so nothing you shared in your first months quietly turns into a dead link the day you upgrade.

What does a custom domain cost in India in 2026?
The domain itself is cheap — roughly ₹600 to ₹1,200 a year for a .in or .com at mainstream registrars, with renewal usually costing more than the discounted first year. The expensive part is what the domain points at. Course platforms gate custom domains behind monthly plans that run from roughly ₹3,500 a month to well over ₹16,000, and a self-hosted WordPress stack adds hosting, plugin licences and maintenance on top. On AllCoaching it is included in every plan: Starter at ₹6,999 a year, or Growth at ₹7,999 a month and Pro at ₹14,999 a month with 0% commission.

Is a custom domain included free on AllCoaching, or is it a paid feature?
Getting started is Starter at ₹6,999 a year. No setup fee, and a 10% platform fee only on what you sell, so you keep 90%; or choose Growth at ₹7,999 a month or Pro at ₹14,999 a month with 0% commission, so you keep 100%. A free allcoaching.in web address is included with every plan and renews with it. Connecting a domain you own is included in every plan, along with courses, tests, notes, student logins and an installable phone app. After it, the only ongoing cost on Starter is the same 90/10 split on what you actually sell; on Growth and Pro you keep 100%.

Is a coaching website on my own domain secure enough to sell paid courses?
It depends entirely on what sits behind the address, not on the address. The questions worth asking any provider are whether HTTPS is issued and renewed automatically, whether lecture and PDF access is bound to a logged-in student rather than a shareable link, whether card details ever touch the seller's own systems, and whether student data can be exported and deleted on request under the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023. A domain with a padlock and an open Drive folder behind it is not secure.

Will moving to my own domain hurt my Google rankings?
Only if it is done carelessly. Google's own site-move guidance is to redirect old URLs to their new equivalents, keep those redirects in place for at least a year, and file a Change of Address in Search Console for every verified variant of the old address. Done that way, ranking signals transfer. Moving early, while the old address has little accumulated authority to lose, is by far the cheapest time to do it.

Are live classes included in the ₹6,999, or charged separately?
Included. Every plan, from ₹6,999 a year, covers the whole academy — the studio, your website, the student app on your own domain, recorded courses, PDF notes, test series and live classes. There is no separate live plan and no per-hour meter. On Starter the only other money that moves is a 10% platform fee on what you actually sell, so you keep 90%; on Growth and Pro the commission is 0%, so you keep 100%.

## Why educators look for an alternative to a custom-built app

Most educators who search for an alternative already have an app, or a quote for one, and something about it is not working. The reasons usually fall into three groups.



### 1. Every change needs a developer

A custom app does what it was built to do on launch day. Adding a new batch type, changing a price page or fixing a bug after an Android update means going back to the developer, and paying again.



### 2. The app is only one piece

An app on its own does not take payments, host live classes, run tests or give you a website on your own domain unless each was built in. Educators end up running the app alongside WhatsApp, Zoom, Google Forms and UPI screenshots.


Question educators ask



### Is building a personal coaching app a mistake?

No. Having your own app is a strong asset for a coaching brand. The mistake is owning one you cannot change yourself, cannot afford to keep updated, or that runs without payments, tests and a website around it.




### 3. Nobody downloads it

An app does not bring students by itself. If downloads are the problem, a new app will not fix it; read why a coaching app gets no students first.



An app of your own works best when everything else lives in the same place.

## Glossary


Personal coaching app
An Android or iOS app that carries one educator's or institute's name, built by an agency or on a platform.
White-label app
An app that carries your brand's name and logo, built on a platform's technology.
App-builder platform
A vendor that sets up a branded app for you on its own technology, usually on a yearly plan.
Developer account
The Google Play or Apple account an app is published under. Whoever owns it controls the listing.
Educator marketplace
One app that lists many educators' courses so students can browse and buy from them.

# Will Free Government Coaching Hurt My Coaching Institute? (2026)

**Source:** https://allcoaching.in/blog/free-government-coaching-impact-on-private-educators  
**Published:** 2026-08-15  
**Updated:** 2026-08-15  
**Author:** Amit Ratan, Founder &amp; CEO, AllCoaching  

**Summary:** PM Modi announced free online coaching on 15 August 2026. What it actually means for private coaching educators in India, who is genuinely at risk, and what to do next.

In this article


- The reframe: cost, not competition.

- What was actually said — and what was not.

- Free has been your competitor for a decade.

- What an Indian family actually pays you for.

- Who is genuinely at risk — honestly.

- Who this may quietly help.

- The DPI clause, and why educators should read it twice.

- The 7-step response for the next 12 months.

- The constraint that decides your outcome.

- Three myths circulating since the speech.

- The verdict.

- References and sources.

- Glossary — key terms.

- Frequently asked questions.






Key Takeaways — the entire analysis in 7 facts:

- On 15 August 2026 the Prime Minister announced free online coaching for competitive exams, citing the burden on poor and middle-class families.

- No implementation detail exists yet — no scheme name, mechanism, timeline, eligibility or exam list has been published.

- The stated mechanism is DPI plus teachers — shared digital rails connecting India's educators, not a single government institute.

- Free supply is not new — YouTube, SWAYAM, DIKSHA and NCERT have been free for years without displacing paid coaching.

- Families pay for accountability, not information — structure, correction and personal attention are what free content cannot supply.

- The exposed model is content-as-product — large impersonal batches priced on access to recorded lectures, not on outcomes.

- Discovery remains the binding constraint — for most capable educators the problem was never teaching quality, it was being found.

Where we are · 2026

AllCoaching is an LMS you build yourself — drag and drop your courses, tests, notes and live classes, then make it your brand with your own domain, logo and Android app (iOS app on Pro). 500+ educators across India already sell through it. Every plan starts with a 7-day free trial, and the price is on the page before you sign up.

Start your 7-day free trial
No card needed · 0% commission on Growth and Pro · Plans from ₹6,999/year

The reframe

## This was an announcement
about cost, not competition.

Free government coaching, announced on 15 August 2026, is unlikely to displace private coaching in India — but it will accelerate the commoditisation of one specific business model within it: the one that sells recorded syllabus coverage to large impersonal batches and justifies its price by access to material rather than by responsibility for a result. If that is not your model, the announcement changes your competitive position far less than the last two days of commentary suggests.

Read the Prime Minister's actual words carefully, because the framing matters. The statement was "coaching classes burden the poor and the middle class" — a sentence about household financial strain, not about the quality or legitimacy of private teaching. The problem being addressed is that families who cannot afford coaching feel they must buy it anyway. That is a cost-of-access problem, and the intervention aims at students who are currently priced out — students who, by definition, were not paying you.

Almost every anxious conversation happening among coaching owners this week collapses those two things: an announcement about affordability is being processed as an announcement about competition. They are different. A public provision aimed at people who cannot pay does not automatically take customers from people who can and do. It changes the floor of the market, not necessarily its middle. Whether it touches you depends entirely on what, precisely, your students are paying for — which is the question the rest of this analysis is built around.

· · ·

The record

## What was actually said —
and what was not.

Precision here is worth more than speed, because a great deal of confident commentary is currently being extrapolated from a small number of sentences. In his Independence Day address from the Red Fort — the 80th Independence Day, his thirteenth consecutive address, delivered under the theme Yuva Shakti for Viksit Bharat@2047 — the Prime Minister announced free online coaching for competitive examinations[1].

"Coaching classes burden the poor and the middle class. We will provide free online coaching for various exams."

— Prime Minister Narendra Modi, Independence Day address, 15 August 2026, as reported

Reported alongside it were three further points worth holding onto. First, the reasoning: intense competition around coaching has become a serious financial burden on middle-class families, with parents feeling that not sending a child to coaching means the child falls behind[2]. Second, the mechanism: the government would draw on India's digital public infrastructure together with its pool of teachers and educators to deliver the initiative[3]. Third, the surrounding context: the same address committed to training one crore young people in artificial intelligence over the following year.

What has not been announced, at the time of writing: a scheme name, the delivery mechanism in any operational detail, a timeline, eligibility criteria, which examinations are covered, how teachers would be selected or compensated, or how it interacts with existing platforms. Any article telling you confidently what this will do to your admissions is guessing.

This absence is not a criticism — Independence Day addresses state direction, and ministries publish specifics later. But it should govern how you respond. Plan for the direction of travel; do not restructure your institute around details that do not yet exist. The direction of travel is clear enough on its own: the state considers the cost of exam preparation a public problem, and intends to use shared digital rails and existing teachers rather than build a single central institute. Both halves of that matter, and the second half is the one educators are under-reading.

· · ·

The precedent

## Free has been your competitor
for a decade.

The single most useful corrective to this week's anxiety is historical. Free, high-quality educational content has existed at enormous scale in India for more than a decade, and paid coaching grew anyway. This is not a prediction; it is the record. Any theory that free supply destroys paid coaching has to explain why it has not already happened.

Consider what is already free and has been for years. NCERT textbooks — the actual foundation of most competitive syllabi — are freely available. SWAYAM hosts free courses spanning school to higher education, built by the Government of India. DIKSHA serves school content nationally. And beyond government provision, YouTube contains more free JEE, NEET, UPSC and SSC instruction than any student could consume in a lifetime, much of it taught by genuinely excellent teachers. A motivated student with a smartphone has had free access to world-class instruction for years.

And yet Indian families kept paying. Not because they were unaware of the free options — they were entirely aware — but because free content solved a problem they did not have. They did not lack access to explanations. They lacked something else, and identifying that something is the whole of a coaching educator's defensibility.

Question Often Asked

### If free YouTube coaching never hurt us, why would government free coaching be different?

In three ways it could be, and it is worth being honest about them rather than dismissing the question. First, trust and legitimacy — a government-backed offering carries an institutional credibility that an unknown YouTube channel does not, particularly for parents in smaller towns who are cautious about online learning. Second, structure — if the initiative delivers organised, sequenced, exam-specific programmes rather than scattered videos, it addresses the main weakness of free content, which has always been that students do not know what to watch in what order. Third, scale of awareness — a national announcement reaches families who never searched for free alternatives at all. Those are real differences and a serious educator should account for them. What none of them changes is the core limitation: a national free programme, however well built, cannot be personally answerable for one student's result. It can teach a million students; it cannot notice that one of them stopped submitting tests in October — and noticing exactly that is the discipline examined in reducing student dropout in online coaching.

· · ·

The real product

## What an Indian family
actually pays you for.

Ask a parent in Kanpur or Patna why they pay coaching fees and the answer is almost never "for the lectures". They are buying accountability — the reasonable expectation that a named adult is paying attention to their specific child and will notice when something goes wrong. The syllabus explanation is the visible part of the transaction. It is not the valuable part, and it has not been the valuable part for years.

Break down what actually transfers when a student joins a good coaching class. There is structure — a sequence, a calendar, a decision about what to study when, which removes the paralysing question of where to start. There is correction — someone who sees the mistake in the student's method, not just the wrong answer, and intervenes. There is discipline — the simple, underrated fact that a fixed class at a fixed hour with a teacher who notices absence produces attendance that a free video library never will. And there is social accountability — peers, ranks, a teacher's expectation.

What free content supplies well

Explanation of concepts · syllabus coverage · worked examples · revision material · exam-pattern familiarity · unlimited repetition at zero marginal cost.

What free content structurally cannot supply

Personal accountability for one student's result · noticing when a specific student disengages · correcting an individual's method rather than their answer · a relationship a family trusts · the discipline of being expected somewhere at a fixed time.

This distinction is the entire strategic question, and it is worth stating as a test: if a student could replace your course with a free playlist and lose nothing, you were selling information. If they would lose the thing that actually makes them study — attention, correction, expectation — you were selling accountability, and free supply does not reach it. Most genuinely good educators are in the second category and have simply never articulated it, which is why they feel threatened by every announcement of free content. The economics of pricing that value are worked through in how to price online courses in India.

· · ·

The honest part

## Who is genuinely
at risk.

A comforting article would stop at "nothing changes". That would be dishonest, and educators deserve better. There is a segment of Indian coaching for which this announcement is a real, structural threat, and naming it plainly is more useful than reassurance.

The exposed model has a recognisable shape. It sells recorded syllabus coverage as its primary product. It runs large batches where no individual student is known by the teacher. Its pricing is justified by access — you pay to get the lectures — rather than by outcomes or attention. And it competes chiefly on being cheaper than the larger branded player rather than on being better than anyone. For that operator, a credible free national alternative attacks the only axis on which they were competing, and price is not an axis you can defend against free.



Exposed

Content-as-product. Recorded lectures, large anonymous batches, price justified by access, competing on being cheaper.



Defensible

Accountability-as-product. Known students, correction and attention, price justified by outcomes, competing on being trusted.




There is a second, subtler exposure worth flagging: the institute whose enrolment depends on being the only visible option in its locality. Geographic monopoly has quietly protected a great many coaching centres — not because they were the best available teaching, but because they were the available teaching. Every expansion of credible online supply, free or paid, erodes that protection a little further. This has been happening for years and this announcement continues it rather than starting it. The response is not to resist it but to stop depending on it, a shift discussed in migrating offline coaching online at zero cost.

· · ·

The other side

## Who this may
quietly help.

Large expansions of free supply have a consistent second-order effect that is easy to miss: they grow the population comfortable with the format. When a national initiative tells millions of families that serious exam preparation happens online, it normalises online learning for households that would never otherwise have tried it — and a meaningful share of those families, having started free, will pay for more attention once they are convinced the format works.

This is the pattern seen wherever free plans meet paid markets, and India's own recent history supports it. The years of free YouTube instruction did not shrink the paid coaching market; they expanded the number of people who believed online learning was legitimate, and the paid market grew alongside. Free supply tends to convert non-consumers into consumers, and only a portion of those stop at free. The educator positioned to receive that overflow — visible, credible, offering the attention that free provision cannot — is a beneficiary rather than a casualty.

There is also a compositional effect. When basic content is free and abundant, the question a student asks shifts from "where can I get the material" to "who should I learn from". That is a question about the teacher, not the institution — and it is a far better question for an individually excellent educator than for a brand whose advantage was advertising budget. Abundance of content moves the competition onto ground where a genuinely good teacher wins. Building the recognition that lets a student answer that question in your favour is the work described in building a personal brand as an educator in India, and the practical routes to first paid students without ad spend are in how to get paid students for online coaching free.

Free content does not compete with a great teacher. It competes with a mediocre institution that was charging for access to information — and it removes the cover that institution was hiding behind.

· · ·

The clause to reread

## The DPI clause, and why
educators should read it twice.

The most consequential phrase in the announcement is not "free" — it is the delivery mechanism. The government said it would draw on India's digital public infrastructure together with its pool of teachers and educators[3]. That is a structural statement, and it deserves more attention than the headline.

Digital public infrastructure means shared, open rails built as public utilities — the architectural approach India has used at national scale for identity and payments. The defining property of that approach is that it does not replace private providers; it connects them. Payments infrastructure did not eliminate banks and merchants — it made it possible for millions of small participants to transact on common rails, and the biggest beneficiaries were the smallest players, who gained reach they could never have built alone.

Applied to education, the same logic points somewhere specific. A DPI-shaped approach to coaching implies connecting India's existing teachers through shared infrastructure rather than employing a few of them in a central institution. It is a networked answer, not a monopoly answer. And a networked answer requires exactly one thing from an individual educator: to be discoverable and structured enough to be connected to. An educator who exists only as an offline classroom, or as an isolated personal app nobody can find, is not connectable by any network, public or private.

Question Often Asked

### Should I wait to see the scheme's details before changing anything about my coaching?

Wait before restructuring; do not wait before strengthening. The distinction matters. Any decision that depends on the scheme's specifics — pricing overhauls, changing your exam focus, closing a centre — should absolutely wait, because no scheme name, mechanism, timeline or exam list has been published, and acting on speculation is how institutes make expensive mistakes. But the actions worth taking are ones you would want regardless of what the scheme turns out to be: knowing your students individually, being able to prove your results, making sure a student searching for your subject in your city can find you, and being discoverable on more than one channel. None of those becomes wrong under any version of the scheme, and all of them take months to build — which is why starting them now and deciding later is the correct sequence rather than a contradiction.

· · ·

The response

## The 7-step response for
the next 12 months.

None of these depends on the scheme's details. All of them are worth doing whatever it turns out to be — which is precisely why they are the right things to start now.

1Step 01

### Audit what is information and what is accountability

List everything a student pays you for. Mark each as information (replicable by any free platform) or accountability (not replicable). The ratio tells you your actual exposure.

2Step 02

### Name the outcome you own

Free platforms serve everyone and are answerable for no one. State which exam, which cohort and which result your teaching is accountable for — that sentence is your defensibility.

3Step 03

### Shift from batch size to attention density

Competing on cheapest-large-batch is competing on the axis free supply attacks. Smaller cohorts with real attention are harder to replicate and hold their price.

4Step 04

### Build visible, honest proof

Improvement records, selections, consented testimonials. When content is abundant, proof is the scarce currency — and it is the thing no free platform can borrow from you.

5Step 05

### Fix discovery before capacity

Most capable educators do not have a teaching problem; they have a being-found problem. Make sure students searching your subject and city can reach you without you buying ads.

6Step 06

### Reprice on outcome, not on access

If your fee is justified by access to lectures, free supply erodes it. If it is justified by attention and accountability, it holds. Say so explicitly to parents.

7Step 07

### Review when details are published

Follow the Ministry of Education for specifics rather than headlines, then revisit this assessment. Adjust to facts, not to speculation.

· · ·

The binding constraint

## The constraint that
decides your outcome.

Underneath every version of this question sits one constraint that has decided Indian educators' fortunes for a decade, and it is not content and not price. It is discovery — whether a student who does not already know you can find you. The announcement changes the content landscape. It does not change the fact that a superb teacher in Prayagraj is invisible to a student in Ranchi who would have paid them gladly.

This is where a great deal of well-intentioned advice fails educators. Being told to "improve quality" is useless to someone whose quality was never the problem — and in our experience across the AllCoaching educator base in 2026, it rarely is. The teachers we onboard are typically excellent and typically unknown. They spent ₹30,000–40,000 on a personal app that became, in the manifesto's phrase, an island: built, branded, and completely undiscoverable. The app was never the missing piece. The street outside it was — the failure mode diagnosed in why your coaching app is not getting students.

A marketplace answers that specific constraint, and it is why AllCoaching is built as one rather than as another app builder. An educator gets a branded studio and app under their own name, and is simultaneously discoverable by students browsing a shared marketplace — so being found does not require an advertising budget. The commercial structure follows: ₹6,999/year (Starter plan) with no setup fee, and a 10% platform fee on Starter or 0% commission on Growth and Pro charged only on what you actually sell, so you keep 90% or 100%. When a student pins an educator's profile, that educator becomes their study space rather than one tab among many.

Where this connects back to the announcement: if the state's own stated approach is to link India's teachers through shared digital rails, then the educators who benefit are the ones who are connectable — visible, structured, with a real presence students can reach. That is worth building whether the connecting layer turns out to be public, private, or both. It is the same preparation either way.

To be straightforward about the boundary: AllCoaching is infrastructure for educators who charge for their teaching, and a free public initiative serves students who cannot pay. Those are different needs and we are not competing with the government's stated goal. The relevant point for an educator is narrower and more practical — in a market where content is abundant and free, the scarce assets are trust, attention and discoverability, and only the last of those can be supplied by a platform.

· · ·

The myths

## Three myths circulating
since the speech.

Three claims have spread quickly this week, and each misreads what was said.



Myth

"The government is going to shut down private coaching."



Reality

Nothing announced restricts private coaching. The statement was about providing a free option for families burdened by cost, not about prohibiting paid teaching.




The second myth is "we should cut fees immediately" — a reflex that damages economics permanently in response to a scheme whose details do not yet exist. Discounting is the right answer only if your offering genuinely competes on access to content, in which case the offering is the problem and the price is a symptom. The third is "this only affects the big edtech brands" — comforting and wrong in the opposite direction, because a large brand has capital and distribution to absorb a shock, while a small centre competing purely on being the cheapest local source of lectures has neither. Exposure follows business model, not size.

· · ·

The verdict

## The verdict.

So the honest answer to whether free government coaching will hurt your coaching institute is: it depends on what you were actually selling, and most educators have never been forced to answer that precisely. If you were selling access to information, the answer is yes, and it was already becoming yes before 15 August — NCERT, SWAYAM, DIKSHA and a decade of free YouTube instruction had been eroding that position for years. If you were selling accountability for a specific student's result, the answer is no, because no national programme, however well funded, can be answerable for one child.

What the announcement genuinely does is remove an excuse. For years, a coaching centre could survive on being the only visible option locally, or on being slightly cheaper than a big brand, without ever articulating what it was actually worth. An abundant free alternative makes that articulation compulsory. That is uncomfortable, and it is also the most useful thing that could happen to an educator who is genuinely good and has simply never had to say why.

And read the mechanism once more before deciding how to feel. The stated approach is to connect India's teachers through shared digital rails — a networked answer that requires individual educators to be discoverable, not a central institution that replaces them. The educators who do well over the next decade will be the ones who are findable on their merit rather than their marketing budget. That was true before this speech; the speech simply made it national policy language.

- Do not restructure on speculation — no scheme name, mechanism, timeline or exam list has been published.

- Do audit information versus accountability — the ratio is your real exposure.

- Do not cut fees reflexively — discounting is a symptom fix for a positioning problem.

- Do build proof of outcomes — the scarce currency when content is abundant.

- Do fix discovery now — it takes months and is right under every scenario.

- Do follow the Ministry of Education for actual details rather than commentary.

A good teacher has never been at risk from more education existing. They have only ever been at risk from nobody finding them. This article is independent analysis for educators, not an official description of any government scheme.

"India never had a shortage of great teachers. It had a shortage of ways for a great teacher to be found without a crore-rupee marketing budget. Every policy that makes education more abundant makes that shortage more visible — and more worth solving."

— Amit Ratan, Founder & CEO, AllCoaching
