The best app for a home tutor to manage students and fees is the one that keeps students, batches, dues and communication in a single place — because a home tutor's real problem is never any one of those individually, it is that they are scattered across five systems that cannot talk to each other. Almost every tool marketed to tutors solves one slice well: a fee tracker, a scheduling app, a payment link, a notes-sharing tool. Adding a sixth system to five that are already fragmented does not reduce the work; it increases it. The question worth asking is not which app tracks fees best, but which single place can hold the whole operation.

It is worth being precise about who this is for, because the advice differs sharply by scale. A coaching institute with two hundred students, staff, and multiple teachers has an administrative problem and genuinely needs institute software; that case is covered separately in our guide to a coaching institute fee collection and receipt app. A home tutor has a different problem entirely: there is no administration, because you are the administration. You teach, you schedule, you collect, you remind, and you also happen to be the person who feels awkward asking a parent for last month's fee. Software built for an institute assumes a separation between teaching and collecting that simply does not exist in your day.

Across the educators onboarding on AllCoaching in 2026, the individual tutors consistently arrive with the same two sentences: "I don't know exactly who owes me money" and "I keep forgetting to ask". Those are not complaints about software. They are the symptoms of an operation whose records live partly in a diary and mostly in a head — and they are why a home tutor's income is often smaller than their student list suggests it should be. This guide is about closing that gap, without buying anything.





Key Takeaways — the entire post in six facts:


- Six fields cover everything a home tutor needs — name and class, parent contact, days and timing, fee and cycle, outstanding amount, and a progress note. The rest is software offering you fields you will not use.

- The diary breaks between 15 and 25 students — not loudly, but by degrading: partial payments forgotten, reminders unsure, same-name students confused, dues left unasked.

- Outstanding dues is the one number you cannot be unsure about — and it is precisely the number a notebook and a chat thread report least reliably.

- Institute software is priced for institutes — the smallest tier commonly runs ₹500–₹2,000 per month plus a setup charge, for features built around staff you do not have.

- Automating the reminder solves an emotional problem, not a technical one — most unpaid tuition in India is not refusal, it is something nobody asked about at the right moment.

## Why Your Business Lives in Five Places

Before choosing anything, it helps to see the current system clearly, because most home tutors have never actually looked at it as a system. Nothing here was a decision; each piece was added at the moment it was needed, and together they became the way the business runs.




Where the information actually sits

The diary holds who comes when · WhatsApp holds what was agreed and promised · the UPI app holds what arrived · a notebook or loose sheet holds who paid · and your memory holds the exceptions, the adjustments, and the parent you must not annoy.



What that costs you

No place answers "what does this student owe today" · reminders depend on you remembering to remember · a payment arrives labelled with a payer name, not a student · and every exception you are holding in your head is a small tax on attention you would rather spend teaching.





The failure mode is not that any one piece is bad. It is that no two of them agree, and reconciling them is a manual act you perform in your head, several times a day. A parent's message saying they will pay next week lives in WhatsApp; the ₹3,000 that arrives eleven days later lives in your UPI app under a name that may be the father's, the mother's, or an uncle's; the fact that it was a partial payment against ₹4,500 lives nowhere at all except in your recollection. Multiply that by thirty students and the arithmetic stops being possible to hold.

This is why the useful frame is a single source of truth rather than "a fee app". You are not looking for a better calculator. You are looking for one place where the student, the schedule, the agreed fee, the payments received and the balance outstanding sit in the same record, so that the question has this student paid for August has exactly one answer, and finding it takes a second rather than a scroll.


Question Often Asked



### My system works fine. Why change something that isn't broken?

If it genuinely works, do not change it — this is not a problem you should solve pre-emptively at ten students. The honest test is not whether it works but whether you can answer three questions in under a minute: who owes me money right now, how much in total, and who was last reminded. If you can, your system is fine at your current size. If you cannot, the system is already failing and you have adapted to it, which is a different thing from it working. The reason to act before it hurts is switching cost: moving twelve students takes an afternoon; moving forty takes a weekend, and you will be doing it in the month you are busiest.




· · ·





## The Six Things Worth Tracking (and What to Ignore)

Software companies sell home tutors far more fields than they will ever fill. Attendance biometrics, performance dashboards, parent portals, homework submission workflows — all real features, almost none of them used by someone teaching twenty-five students alone. The list below is what a solo tutor actually needs, and it is deliberately short.


1

The record



### Name, class or exam, and parent contact

The identity of the student and the person who pays — which is often not the same person. Record the parent's number separately from the student's, because fee conversations go to one and study conversations to the other, and mixing them is how reminders end up ignored.





2

The schedule



### Days, timing, and location or mode

When you teach them and where — at their home, at yours, or online. This is the field that prevents the most expensive mistake a home tutor makes: double-booking a slot and losing a student over it, which costs more than a full year of any software.





3

The money



### Agreed fee, fee cycle, and outstanding dues

What they pay, when it falls due, and what remains unpaid today. Outstanding dues is the single most important number in your entire operation, and the one that a diary reports least reliably — because a diary records events, not balances.





4

The relationship



### A short progress or attendance note

Two lines after each month: what improved, what is stuck, how regular they were. This is what makes a renewal conversation easy and a parent complaint answerable, and it is the raw material for the update that keeps parents paying without being asked twice.




What to leave out is equally important. Do not track anything you will not look at within thirty days. Detailed per-topic scores, elaborate attendance percentages, and multi-field parent profiles are collected diligently for three weeks and abandoned in the fourth, and the abandoned fields then make the whole record look untrustworthy. If you want deeper measurement later, the case for it is laid out in student progress tracking tools for coaching — but it is a second-year problem, not a first-month one.



· · ·





## The Breaking Point — Where the Diary Fails

The diary-and-WhatsApp system does not collapse. It degrades, which is far more dangerous, because degradation is easy to absorb and hard to notice. Somewhere between fifteen and twenty-five students, depending on how many batches and fee dates you juggle, the following starts happening — and each symptom is usually blamed on being busy rather than on the system.


The five symptoms of a system past its limit


- You are not certain who has paid. You have a feeling, and you are usually right, and "usually" is where the leakage lives.

- Partial payments stop being tracked. ₹2,000 against a ₹3,500 fee becomes "he paid" in your memory and a ₹1,500 hole in your income.

- You delay asking. Not because you forgot, but because asking is uncomfortable, and a month of discomfort becomes a quarter of unpaid dues.

- Two students blur together. Same first name, different batches, and a payment gets credited against the wrong one.

- You stop knowing your own income. You can state your fee per student and your student count, but not what you actually collected last month.




Look at that list and notice what it has in common: every one of them is a memory failure, not a discipline failure. Home tutors routinely interpret these symptoms as personal shortcomings — being disorganised, being too soft about money — and respond by resolving to try harder. Trying harder does not work, because the problem is that you are being asked to hold state in your head that no one can hold reliably past a couple of dozen students. The fix is structural: move the state out of your head and into a record.


Question Often Asked



### How much money does a disorganised home tutor actually lose?

There is no honest universal figure, and anyone quoting one precisely is guessing — but the shape of the loss is predictable, and you can calculate your own in two minutes. Take your monthly fee, multiply by the number of students carrying unpaid or partial dues right now, and multiply by how many months those dues have been outstanding. For a tutor charging ₹2,500 a month with four students two months behind, that is ₹20,000 sitting uncollected — usually not because anyone refused, but because nobody was asked at the right moment. The point is not the number; it is that the number exists and you probably cannot state it, which is itself the finding.




· · ·





## Fees: The Part That Quietly Leaks

Fee collection deserves its own treatment because it is where a home tutor's system fails most expensively, and because the failure has an emotional component that no feature list acknowledges. Collecting is not hard technically — UPI solved that years ago. It is hard socially, and the software's real job is to remove you from the awkward part.

Consider what happens on a personal UPI QR, which is how most home tutors collect today. A credit arrives. It tells you an amount and a payer name, and nothing else — not which student, not which month, not whether it clears the balance or only part of it. If the payer is a parent whose surname differs from the student's, or a sibling paying on behalf, even the identification is guesswork. You then perform reconciliation manually, in your head, and record the result in a notebook that has no link back to the payment. Every step there is an opportunity for the number to drift.

The alternative is not a different payment app; it is a payment tied to a student record. When the request goes out against a student and a fee cycle, the money arrives already labelled — this student, this month, this much remaining. Reconciliation stops being a task because it happened at the moment of payment. That single architectural difference is what separates a fee app from a payments app, and it is the thing worth actually paying attention to when comparing options.


The reminder is the feature, not the ledger. Most unpaid tuition in India is not refusal — it is a parent who intended to pay, got busy, and was never reminded at a moment when paying was convenient. A short automated message three days before the due date, and one three days after, collects more than any amount of resolve to "be firmer about fees". It works because it is on time, and because it is the system asking rather than you.



One practical note on records and tax, which should not become a reason to delay. Tuition income is income, and as it grows it may cross registration thresholds. That is a growth problem rather than a starting problem — but it is far cheaper to keep clean records from your first student than to reconstruct a year of cash payments later. The specifics for individual tutors are covered in online tutor GST and income tax in India, and the boundary between a simple fee receipt and a tax invoice is worth confirming with a chartered accountant rather than assuming your software gets it right.



· · ·

## How to Choose — and What to Ignore

Whatever you end up using, judge it on a short list. Most tutor software is sold on breadth, and breadth is precisely what a solo operator does not need — every additional module is another thing to maintain and another reason to abandon the system in month two.


Five questions that decide it


- Can I see what one student owes in one tap? If it takes a report, a filter, or arithmetic, it will not survive a busy week.

- Does a payment arrive already labelled? Tied to student and month, or you are still reconciling by hand.

- Do reminders go out without me? The automation is the product; the ledger is table stakes.

- Can I set it up alone, on a phone, in an evening? If onboarding needs a call or a training session, it was built for staff you do not have.

- What does it cost in a month when I sell nothing? A fixed monthly bill is most painful in exactly the months you can least afford it.




Ignore, meanwhile, almost everything sold as a differentiator. Biometric attendance, parent mobile apps, elaborate analytics dashboards and homework-submission workflows are institute features, and for a solo tutor they are administrative weight without an administrator to carry it. The same applies to building anything custom: a bespoke app runs ₹4–11 lakh in the first year once maintenance is counted, as broken down in white-label coaching app development cost in India, and it would not manage your students any better than a studio does.


Question Often Asked



### Should I use a general tool like Google Sheets instead of tutor software?

A spreadsheet is a genuinely good ledger and a genuinely bad system, and knowing the difference saves months. It will hold your students and compute your dues perfectly well — what it cannot do is act. It will not send a reminder, will not collect a payment, will not tie an incoming ₹3,000 to a student, and will not do anything at all on a week when you are too busy to open it. That last point is decisive: the whole reason to leave the diary is to stop being the single point of failure, and a spreadsheet keeps you exactly that. Use one if you like maintaining it; just do not expect it to fix the asking problem, which is the one actually costing you money.




· · ·





## The One-Weekend Rollout

Moving off the diary is a weekend of work, not a project, and it is worth doing in one sitting rather than gradually — a half-migrated system is worse than either the old one or the new one, because now the truth is in two places.


1

Saturday morning · 60–90 minutes



### List every student in one place

Go through the diary, your phone contacts, and your memory, and write down every current student with name, class or exam, parent contact, days and timing, and the agreed fee. This list is the asset — everything after this is mechanical. Expect to find two or three students you had half-forgotten.





2

Saturday afternoon · 30 minutes



### Define batches and fee cycles

Group students into the batches you really teach — by class, by subject, or simply by slot — and set each one's fee cycle, usually monthly on a fixed date. Grouping is what turns twenty separate arrangements into four repeatable ones, and it is the step that makes reminders possible to automate.





3

Saturday evening · the uncomfortable hour



### Enter opening dues honestly

Record what each student actually owes today, including partial payments and the informal adjustments you have been carrying in your head. Resist the urge to round it kindly. A clean opening balance is what makes every number after it trustworthy, and this is the only time you will have to do it.





4

Sunday morning · 20 minutes



### Switch collection to a payment link

Stop sending a personal UPI QR and start sending a payment link tied to the student record. Money then arrives already labelled with student, month and remaining balance, and settles to your bank automatically. Tell parents once, in a single message; nobody objects to a link that works.





5

Sunday afternoon · 10 minutes



### Turn on automated reminders

Schedule one reminder a few days before the due date and one a few days after, going to the parent's number automatically. This is the step that actually changes your income, because it removes you from the asking — and the asking, not the tracking, is what has been costing you money.




By Sunday evening the operation that lived in five places lives in one, and the questions that used to require a scroll now take a second. The part most tutors underestimate is how much attention this frees: the exceptions you were holding in your head — who is behind, who promised what, who to avoid annoying — are now written down, and you can stop carrying them.

## The Strategic Conclusion

We opened by saying the best app for a home tutor is the one that holds students, batches, dues and communication in a single place, and with the full picture in view that holds precisely. The failure a home tutor experiences is almost never a teaching failure and almost never a discipline failure. It is a state-keeping failure — an operation asking one person to remember more than any person can, and then blaming that person when a fee goes uncollected.

Across the individual tutors we work with at AllCoaching, the ones whose income matches their student list share a recognisable pattern. They have:


- One place instead of five — student, schedule, fee and payment in the same record, so no two sources can disagree.

- Tracked six fields, not sixteen — and therefore still use the system in month six.

- Made outstanding dues visible rather than remembered, because it is the one number that cannot be approximate.

- Automated the asking, which converts an emotional problem into a scheduled one.

- Refused to buy institute software for a one-person operation, and refused to build anything custom.



The wider context makes the timing favourable rather than urgent. India's online education segment is compounding at close to 20% a year[2] within an edtech market projected to reach ₹2,50,850 crore (US$ 29 billion) by 2030[1], and the individual tutor is the unit best positioned to benefit — provided their operation can absorb more students without their memory being the constraint. Organising is not administrative work; it is what makes growth survivable.

So the next action is small and finite. Take one hour this weekend and write down every student with what they owe you. You will almost certainly find money you had forgotten to ask for, and that alone usually pays for the effort. Then open studio.allcoaching.in, set up your studio with a single OTP, move that list in, and switch on the reminders. By Sunday evening you will be able to answer, in one second, the question you currently answer with a feeling.

## Glossary — Key Terms


Term



### Home Tutor

An individual who teaches students privately — at the student's home, their own home, or online — and manages the entire operation alone. Distinct from a coaching institute, which has staff, multiple teachers, and administrative separation between teaching and collection.




Term



### Student CRM

A record for each student holding contact details, batch, schedule, fee cycle, payment history and progress notes. Distinct from a contact list, which stores only a phone number — a CRM answers questions about state, such as what a student owes today.




Term



### Batch

A group of students taught together on a shared schedule, usually defined by class, subject or time slot. Grouping converts many individual arrangements into a few repeatable ones that can be scheduled and billed as a unit.




Term



### Fee Cycle

The repeating interval on which a student's fee falls due, most commonly monthly on a fixed date. Defining it explicitly is what allows reminders and dues to be calculated automatically instead of remembered.




Term



### Outstanding Dues

The amount a student currently owes, after accounting for partial payments and agreed adjustments. It is the single number a tutor cannot afford to be uncertain about, and the one a diary reports least reliably.




Term



### Reconciliation

Matching money received in the bank against the students it was meant for. On a personal UPI account this is manual and error-prone, because a credit shows a payer name but not which student, month or balance it settles.




Term



### Single Source of Truth

One place that holds the authoritative answer to a question, so no two records can disagree. For a home tutor it means student, schedule, fee and payment live together rather than split across a diary, a chat thread and a payments app.




Term



### Branded Studio

A tutor's own white-labelled space carrying their name, where students are enrolled, taught, and billed. Gives the ownership of a custom app without the cost of building one, and works for offline and online students alike.

## Frequently Asked Questions




What is the best app for home tutors to manage students and fees in India?
The best app for a home tutor is the one that keeps students, batches, fees and communication in a single place rather than solving only one of them. Judge any option against five things: a student record with contact and history, a schedule you can see at a glance, per-student dues visible without arithmetic, payment collection tied to that student record, and automated reminders. Institute ERP software does all of this but is built for two hundred students and priced accordingly, typically ₹500–₹2,000 a month plus setup at the smallest tier. A free educator studio such as AllCoaching covers the same ground for an individual tutor from ₹6,999 a year, with UPI and card collection, and a 10% platform fee on Starter or 0% commission on Growth and Pro charged only on what you sell.




Do I need an app if I only have 10 to 15 students?
At ten to fifteen students a diary genuinely works, and anyone telling you otherwise is selling something. The reason to set up a proper system early is not the current headcount but the switching cost later: moving twelve students takes an afternoon, moving forty takes a weekend and you will do it at exactly the moment you are busiest. If your student count is stable and you are not chasing dues, stay with what works. If you are adding students, the cheapest time to organise is now, while the list is short.




Can I manage tuition fees on WhatsApp and a notebook?
Yes, up to a point, and that point arrives somewhere between fifteen and twenty-five students. The system does not fail loudly; it degrades. You start forgetting who paid partially, you stop being sure whether a parent was reminded, two students with the same first name get confused, and you delay asking about dues because asking is uncomfortable. WhatsApp is an excellent communication surface and a poor ledger, because it has no per-student balance, no reliable history, and no way to answer "has this student paid for August" without scrolling.




How much does a student and fee management app cost for a home tutor?
It ranges from ₹0 to roughly ₹25,000 a year depending on what you pick. Institute-focused fee software starts around ₹500–₹2,000 per month at the smallest tier, often with a one-time setup charge, and is built for organisations with staff and multiple batches. A spreadsheet costs nothing in rupees but costs your evenings and offers no reminders or payment collection. An educator studio on a revenue-share model keeps upfront cost low — on AllCoaching the Starter plan is one annual fee with no setup fee, and the platform charges 10% on Starter or 0% commission on Growth and Pro only on what you actually sell.




What should a home tutor track for each student?
Six fields cover almost everything a home tutor needs: name and class or exam, parent contact, days and timing, agreed fee and cycle, amount currently outstanding, and a short note on progress or attendance. Anything beyond that is usually collected because software offers the field, not because the tutor uses it. The two that matter most are outstanding amount, because it is the number you cannot afford to be unsure about, and timing, because scheduling conflicts are what cost a home tutor students.




How do I handle monthly fee reminders without nagging parents?
Make the reminder automatic and impersonal so that it is the system asking rather than you. A short scheduled message a few days before the due date, and one after it passes, works better than a personal message sent when you finally feel frustrated — it arrives on time, sounds like process rather than complaint, and removes the emotional cost that makes tutors delay asking. Most unpaid tuition dues in India are not refusals; they are simply things nobody was reminded about at the right moment.




Can I manage both offline home students and online students in one place?
Yes, and keeping them in one place is the point. A home tutor in 2026 usually has a mix — students who come home or attend at a fixed address, and students taught online — and splitting them across two systems recreates the problem you were solving. A studio that holds the student record, the fee cycle and the payment history works identically for both, and lets you sell a recorded course or a test series to the online half without building anything new.




Do I need GST registration as a home tutor collecting fees?
Not from your first student. GST registration is tied to turnover thresholds and the nature of the supply, and most individual home tutors are well below the point at which registration becomes mandatory. The practical advice is to keep clean records of every fee collected from the beginning, so that if your income grows past the threshold the transition is a formality rather than a reconstruction exercise. For the specifics, including income tax treatment, consult a chartered accountant rather than relying on software defaults.

The best software for live teaching on a digital board is, for most Indian educators, OpenBoard as the writing surface, shared live through your class platform, with every board exported as a PDF page afterwards — a stack that costs nothing. But the software choice is not what decides whether your class works, and treating it as the decision is why so many teachers buy hardware, install three applications, and still lose students in the second week. The variable that actually determines success is smaller and stranger than any feature list: how thick your pen strokes are.

The reason is that a digital board is not a board. It is a video feed, and the person receiving it is almost certainly on a phone. In India that is not a minor demographic detail — mobile is the dominant way students attend online classes, and a board designed on a twenty-four-inch monitor arrives on a six-inch screen at roughly a quarter of the size you were looking at. Everything you found comfortably readable becomes marginal, and everything marginal becomes invisible. The student does not complain about this. They simply stop being able to follow, decide the class is hard, and quietly disengage.

Across the educators onboarding on AllCoaching in 2026, board-teaching problems arrive described as software problems — "which app is best", "should I buy a bigger panel" — and resolve as calibration problems almost every time. This guide covers the software honestly, because the question deserves a real answer, but it puts the calibration first, because that is where the class is actually won or lost.





Key Takeaways — the entire post in six facts:


- The free stack is enough — OpenBoard for writing, your class platform for delivery, PDF export for notes. Paid software rarely fixes what is actually broken.

- Calibrate for a six-inch phone, not your monitor — thicker strokes, larger text, and roughly 6–8 lines per board before turning the page.

- Google Jamboard is discontinued — app and hardware both. Do not build a workflow on it; prefer tools you can export from.

- An interactive flat panel does not improve an online class — a ₹2,500–₹4,500 pen tablet produces the same output on the student's screen.

- Every board is a PDF page you could sell — most teachers erase their entire year of teaching output instead of publishing it as chapter-wise notes.

## Your Student Is Watching on a Phone

Start here, because it reorders every other decision. When you teach on a digital board, you are looking at a large monitor at arm's length with your own handwriting at a comfortable size. Your student is holding a phone, often at a lower video resolution than you are producing, sometimes on a connection that is compressing the feed further. The board that reaches them is a shrunken, softened version of yours.




What you see

A wide, crisp board · your natural handwriting size · fifteen or twenty lines of a derivation visible at once · thin pen strokes that look elegant · small annotations in a corner · colour differences that are obvious.



What the student sees

The same board at roughly a quarter of the size · handwriting near the limit of legibility · a wall of text they cannot parse · thin strokes that break up under compression · corner annotations that are gone · light colours that vanish against white.





The practical fixes are unglamorous and cost nothing. Increase the pen thickness well beyond what looks right to you — on a large monitor a properly calibrated stroke will look slightly crude, and that is the correct setting. Write larger than feels natural. Cap yourself at roughly six to eight lines per board and turn the page rather than shrinking to fit, which is what an infinite canvas is for. Use dark, saturated colours only; light blue and yellow that read fine on your screen disappear entirely after compression.


The one check that fixes most of this. Before your next class, start the session, join it yourself on your own phone, and write a typical line of your subject on the board. Look at your phone, not at your monitor. Adjust stroke weight and size until it is comfortable at arm's length on that phone, then leave those settings alone forever. This takes four minutes and will do more for your teaching than any software upgrade you are considering.




Question Often Asked



### Should I buy a bigger digital board so students can see more?

No — and this is the most expensive misunderstanding in the category. The physical size of your board has no effect whatsoever on what the student sees, because they are not looking at your board; they are looking at its software output, scaled to fit their screen. A seventy-five-inch interactive panel and a small pen tablet produce a pixel-identical feed if the software and settings are the same. Buying a larger panel changes your own comfort while writing, which is a real benefit for in-person classrooms and irrelevant for online ones. If your students cannot see clearly, the fix is stroke weight and lines-per-board, and it is free.




· · ·





## The Three Jobs the Software Must Do

Once calibration is settled, the software question becomes tractable, because a digital-board setup only has to do three things. Most teachers evaluate tools on a jumble of features; evaluating on these three separates the choice cleanly.


1

Job one



### The writing surface

Where you actually write. What matters is an infinite canvas or unlimited pages, so a long derivation never forces you to erase mid-solution; the ability to import a PDF or image and annotate over it, which is how question-solving actually works; and pen behaviour that does not lag.





2

Job two



### Live delivery

How the board reaches the student in real time — either shared directly as a window through your class platform, or composited with your camera into one feed. Simpler is almost always better here, because this is the component that fails five minutes before class.





3

Job three



### Capture and publish

Saving each finished board as an image or PDF page, automatically, and getting those pages to students afterwards. This is the job almost every teacher skips, and it is the one that turns a class into an asset rather than an event that evaporates.




Notice that no single application does all three well, which is why the honest answer to "what software should I use" is a small stack rather than a product name. Whiteboard applications are built for writing and are poor delivery platforms; class platforms are built for delivery and their built-in whiteboards are usually too thin for sustained teaching. Trying to force one tool to do both is the most common source of frustration in this category, and it is worth simply accepting the split.



· · ·





## The Options, Honestly Compared

Here are the realistic choices for the writing surface, judged on the three jobs above rather than on marketing. All of the ones worth recommending are free, which is worth saying plainly because this is a category where teachers routinely assume paid must be better.

OpenBoardFree, open sourceSustained teaching — derivations, PDF annotation, unlimited pagesDesktop only; interface feels dated at first
Microsoft WhiteboardFree with accountDiscussion, quick diagrams, collaborationThin for long structured board work

For most Indian educators teaching a handwriting-heavy subject — mathematics, physics, chemistry, accountancy — OpenBoard is the right default. It is free and open source, it was built for teaching rather than adapted to it, it handles unlimited pages, and critically it lets you import a question paper or textbook page and write over it, which is what solving actually looks like. Its interface is unfashionable and takes an evening to get used to; that is the entire cost.

The row worth pausing on is the last one. Google discontinued Jamboard — both the application and the hardware — and yet it still appears in guides and in teachers' search histories, which means people are building setups on a tool that no longer exists. The broader lesson generalises well beyond this one product: prefer software you can export from. A tool you can export PDFs out of costs you a migration when it shuts down; a tool that locks your boards inside itself costs you your back catalogue. The free recording and whiteboard landscape more broadly is mapped in best free tools for teachers to record lectures.



· · ·





## What Hardware You Actually Need

Hardware deserves a short section rather than a long one, because for online teaching it matters far less than the category's marketing suggests. The full equipment question — camera, microphone, lighting, the whole kit — is worked through in our budget home studio setup for online teaching; here the only question is what you write on.

There are three tiers, and the gap between them is smaller than the price gap implies. A pen tablet — a pad you write on while looking at your monitor — is the entry point, with entry-level options such as the XP-Pen Star G640 and Wacom CTL-472 in the ₹2,500–₹4,500 range. A pen display, where you write directly on a screen, removes the hand-eye separation and costs several times more. An interactive flat panel is a classroom device at classroom prices, and for online teaching it is, as covered above, almost entirely beside the point.


Question Often Asked



### Is a pen tablet hard to get used to?

For most teachers it takes a few hours of real practice, not weeks — but it is genuinely disorienting for the first thirty minutes, and that first half hour is where most people conclude they need to spend more money. The difficulty is hand-eye separation: your hand moves on the pad while your eyes watch the monitor, which your brain resolves surprisingly quickly, in much the same way it resolved using a mouse. The practical advice is to do your adaptation off-air — write out a full lesson's worth of notes on it before you teach a live class on it — so that the awkward phase is not witnessed by students. If it still feels wrong after two weeks of real classes, that is a genuine signal to consider a pen display, and only then.



One caution about touchscreen laptops and tablets used with a finger or a cheap stylus. Without proper palm rejection, resting your hand on the surface produces stray marks, and the constant correction is more disruptive to a class than writing slightly awkwardly on a pad. If you are teaching from a tablet, use its purpose-built stylus. If you do not have one, a ₹2,500 pen tablet attached to a laptop will produce cleaner boards than a finger on a touchscreen, every time.



· · ·





## Wiring It for Live — the Delivery Half

You have a board and something to write with; now it has to reach students while you teach. There are two approaches, and the right one is almost always the less impressive of the two.

Direct window sharing means running your whiteboard application and sharing that window through whatever platform hosts your live class. It is simple, it has the lowest latency, there is nothing extra to configure, and it fails rarely. Compositing means running OBS Studio, arranging board and camera and titles into a designed layout, and sending that single feed. It looks more professional and gives you control that sharing cannot — a camera inset so students see your face while you write, for instance — at the cost of setup effort, CPU load, and one more component that can break at 6:58 pm.


The honest recommendation


- For live classes, share the window directly. Reliability beats production value when thirty students are waiting and you cannot debug.

- For recorded lectures, use OBS Studio. A retake costs nothing, so the extra polish is worth the extra fragility — and OBS is free.

- Learn OBS in a week with no class scheduled, not on the evening you first need it.

- Keep a fallback. Know how to share a plain window if the composited setup fails, and tell students the class will start on time either way.




On the platform that actually hosts the live session, the practical requirement for a board teacher is narrow: students should be able to join on a phone without friction, attendance should be recorded, and the session should be capturable. The mobile-delivery side of that is covered in how to conduct live classes on mobile apps, and it matters more than the board software does — because a student who cannot join reliably never sees your beautifully calibrated strokes at all.



· · ·





## Turn Every Board Into Sellable Notes

This is the section that most digital-board guides omit entirely, and it is the one with money in it. Consider what happens to your boards today: you write them during class, and then they are erased, closed or forgotten. A teacher taking four classes a week produces something like four hundred boards across an academic session, and almost all of them are thrown away.

Those boards are, materially, the thing students most want after class. Not the recording — recordings are long, and a student looking for one step in one derivation will not scrub through ninety minutes to find it. What they want is the page. The chapter, written in your hand, in the order you taught it, in a form they can scroll on the phone they are already holding. That artifact costs you nothing additional to produce, because you already produced it while teaching. It costs only the discipline of exporting it.


"You are already manufacturing the product. The only question is whether you publish it or erase it at the end of every class."



Mechanically this is simple. Set your whiteboard software to export the session — OpenBoard can save a whole session as a PDF document — and make it automatic rather than a thing you remember. Then upload the day's pages into your studio, attached to the batch, so enrolled students get them as part of what they paid for. Over a session this accumulates into a complete chapter-wise handwritten notes set which is genuinely saleable to the next cohort, to students who could not attend, and as a standalone product. How to price and position that is in the best platform for selling PDF notes and test series.

One practical caution, since notes travel further than recordings do. A PDF forwards in one tap, so if these become a paid product, deliver them inside your studio behind a login rather than as files sent on WhatsApp, and consider a watermark carrying the student's name. This does not make sharing impossible — nothing does — but it removes the effortless leak, which is the one that actually costs you. The full picture is in how to protect study material PDFs from sharing.



· · ·





## Five Mistakes That Make a Board Worse Than a Notebook

A digital board is not automatically an upgrade. Used carelessly it is genuinely worse than a teacher writing in a notebook under a phone camera, and the failure modes are consistent enough to list.


What goes wrong, in order of frequency


- Writing at monitor scale. Thin strokes and twenty lines per board. The single biggest cause of silent disengagement.

- Erasing to make room. Wiping the first half of a derivation to fit the second half destroys exactly what the student needed to review. Use pages.

- Filling the board because it is infinite. An unlimited canvas invites sprawl; students following on a phone need short, finished screens.

- Debugging software on air. Every minute spent fixing a layout at the start of class is a minute of attention you do not get back.

- Erasing the year. Teaching four hundred boards across a session and publishing none of them, then starting the next session from zero material.




Read that list and notice that four of the five are habits, not purchases. This is the pattern across the whole category: educators arrive believing they have an equipment problem and leave having fixed a practice problem. The digital board is a genuinely good tool for teaching mathematics and science online — it is faster than a physical board, it never runs out of space, it produces a saveable artifact, and it lets you write over a question paper. All of those advantages are available at the entry price, and all of them are forfeited by the habits above.

If being on camera is the part you are avoiding rather than the writing, that is worth naming separately, because a digital board is the standard solution to it. A board-only class with your voice over it is a completely legitimate format, and for many subjects students prefer it — the approach is set out in how to teach online without showing your face.



· · ·

The board teachers whose classes actually work share a short list of habits. They have:


- Calibrated once on a phone, and never touched the stroke settings again.

- Chosen tools they can export from, so no shutdown takes their back catalogue with it.

- Published every board, ending each session with a chapter-wise notes set instead of an empty folder.

## Glossary — Key Terms


Term



### Digital Board

Any surface a teacher writes on digitally — an interactive flat panel, a pen display, or a pen tablet paired with whiteboard software. For an online class the term describes the software output the student sees, not the physical device, which is why cheap and expensive hardware can look identical on screen.




Term



### Pen Tablet

A drawing pad without a screen, on which the teacher writes while looking at the monitor. Distinct from a pen display, which has its own screen written on directly — the tablet is far cheaper but requires a short adaptation to hand-eye separation.




Term



### Palm Rejection

The ability of a writing surface to ignore the hand resting on it and register only the stylus. Without it, a teacher writing naturally produces stray marks, which is the most common reason a touchscreen makes a poor teaching board.




Term



### Stroke Weight

The thickness of the digital pen line. It is the single most consequential setting in online board teaching, because a stroke calibrated for the teacher's large monitor becomes invisible when the same board is scaled to a student's phone screen.




Term



### Board Capture

Automatically saving each completed board as an image or PDF page during a class. Distinct from screen recording, which captures the session as video — board capture produces static pages that can be sold or shared as notes.




Term



### Compositing

Combining board, camera and audio into a single video feed before sending it to students, usually with software such as OBS Studio. It buys layout control at the cost of setup effort, CPU load, and one more component that can fail before a live class.




Term



### Infinite Canvas

A whiteboard that scrolls or adds pages without limit rather than confining the teacher to one fixed screen. It matters for subjects with long derivations, where running out of board mid-solution forces an erase that destroys the student's ability to review the steps.




Term



### Branded Studio

An educator's own white-labelled space carrying their name, where live classes are scheduled, board notes are published, recordings are hosted and fees are collected. Gives the ownership of a custom app without the cost of building one.

## Frequently Asked Questions




What is the best software for live teaching on a digital board?
For most Indian educators the strongest free combination is OpenBoard as the writing surface, shared live through your class platform, with every board exported as a PDF page afterwards. OpenBoard is open-source, purpose-built for teaching, and handles infinite pages and imported documents, which is what long derivations and question-solving actually need. Microsoft Whiteboard and Excalidraw are lighter and fine for discussion or diagrams but weaker for sustained board work. Add OBS Studio only if you want to composite board, camera and audio into one controlled layout, since it costs setup effort and CPU.




Can I use Google Jamboard for online teaching?
No. Google discontinued Jamboard, both the app and the hardware, so it is not a viable choice for a teaching setup you intend to rely on. Teachers who used it have generally moved to OpenBoard for structured teaching, or to Microsoft Whiteboard and Excalidraw for lighter collaborative work. The wider lesson is worth applying to any tool you build a teaching workflow on: prefer software you can export from, so that a product being shut down costs you a migration rather than your entire back catalogue.




Do I need an expensive interactive flat panel to teach on a digital board?
No. An interactive flat panel is a classroom device sold for classroom budgets, and for a teacher broadcasting to students online it changes almost nothing about what the student sees. A pen tablet at roughly ₹2,500 to ₹4,500 produces an identical result on the student's screen, because the student is watching your software output rather than your physical hardware. Buy the panel if you also teach an in-person room that needs it; do not buy it to improve an online class, because it will not.




Why does my digital board writing look unreadable to students?
Almost always because you are calibrating for your own large monitor while the student is watching on a phone. A board that looks spacious on a 24-inch screen becomes illegible when scaled down to six inches, and the student will not tell you — they will quietly stop following. Fix it by writing thicker strokes, using larger text, and limiting yourself to roughly six to eight lines per board before moving to a new page. Check it once on your own phone before your first class and the problem largely disappears.




Should I use OBS Studio for live classes on a digital board?
Only if you want a specific layout that simple screen sharing cannot give you, such as your board with a small camera inset and a fixed title bar. OBS Studio is free, powerful and genuinely worth learning, but it adds a compositing step, consumes CPU, and introduces one more thing that can fail five minutes before a class. Most teachers are better served by sharing the board window directly for live sessions and reserving OBS for recorded lectures, where a retake costs nothing.




How do I save my digital board as notes for students?
Use your whiteboard software's export function to save each board as an image or a PDF page, and set it to export automatically rather than relying on memory. OpenBoard can export a whole session as a PDF document. Then upload the day's boards into your studio as a chapter-wise notes set attached to the batch. The boards are a by-product you are already producing during class, so publishing them costs almost nothing and turns teaching output into an asset students will pay for.




Is a pen tablet or a pen display better for online teaching?
A pen tablet, where you write on a pad while looking at your monitor, is far cheaper and works well once you have adapted to the hand-eye separation, which usually takes a few hours of practice. A pen display, where you write directly on a screen, removes that adjustment entirely and feels natural immediately, but costs several times more. For a teacher starting out, the honest advice is to begin with an entry-level pen tablet and upgrade only if the separation still bothers you after two weeks of real classes.




Do I need separate software for the board and for the class itself?
Usually yes, and it is worth understanding why. Whiteboard applications are built for writing and are not delivery platforms; class platforms are built for delivery and their built-in whiteboards are typically too limited for sustained teaching. The stack most teachers end up with is a dedicated whiteboard application for the writing, a class platform for the live session and attendance, and a studio where recordings, notes and fees live. On AllCoaching the last of those is included in your plan, so the only tools you need to choose are the first two.

Eight steps, in order. Timeline and prices are illustrative.

- Collect reviews and open batch 2Ask buyers for short reviews, use their doubts to improve the course, then add Meta ads and SEO to fill the next batch.


Notice what is missing: a company registration, an agency-built app, a big ad budget and a 60-hour syllabus. They can come later. Selling is really three jobs: packaging (what outcome, for whom), infrastructure (where the course lives, how money and access work) and distribution (how a stranger finds it). Most educators spend all their energy on the first and barely try the third.






## Step 1: Pick a course people already ask you for

Your first course should be the topic students already ask you about, written as one outcome, for one buyer, in one language. Demand you can see beats an idea you like.

Look at the questions you answer again and again. An SSC maths teacher hears "Percentage aur Profit & Loss ka short trick course banao". A NEET biology tutor gets asked for a chapter-wise test series before the exam. A spoken English trainer hears "I freeze in interviews". A yoga teacher is asked for a 30-day back-pain routine. Each of those is a course waiting to be named.



### Write the offer in one sentence

Include four things: the outcome, the buyer, the language and the time it takes.



Too vagueReady to sell

Maths courseSSC CGL Quant in Hindi: Percentage to Profit & Loss in 30 days
NEET biologyNEET 2027 Biology: chapter-wise tests with video solutions, in Hinglish
English speakingSpoken English for job interviews: 6 weeks of daily practice for freshers
Yoga classes30-day yoga for desk workers with back pain, morning live sessions

Topics describe a syllabus. Outcomes describe what the student gets.


Students buy the removal of a worry (losing marks, freezing in an interview), not coverage of topics. Lead with the result; the syllabus is the proof.

A narrow name is also easier to find: "Class 12 CBSE Physics numericals in Hinglish" matches a real search, while "Complete physics for all classes" competes with everything. If you teach in Hindi, Hinglish or a regional language, put the language in the course name too.






## Step 2: How to validate demand before you record

Validate demand by finding the same request in at least two free places: your YouTube comments, a WhatsApp group poll, Google Trends and search suggestions. Then ask five real students whether they would pay. This takes a day or two and can save weeks of recording.



Check at least two before you record. Logos belong to their owners.



### 1. YouTube comments

Read the comments on your ten most-watched videos (or popular videos in your subject) and count requests for a full course, notes or a test series. "Sir, full course kab aayega?" repeated across videos is a strong signal.



### 2. A WhatsApp group poll

In a group of past or current students, post a poll with two or three options: "Which should the paid batch cover first: Percentage, Ratio or Time and Work?" Keep the options short. Everyone who votes is a likely early buyer.



### 3. Google Trends

Compare two topics or exams over the last 12 months in India. Google Trends does not show search counts; Google explains that each data point is divided by total searches for that place and time and then "scaled on a range of 0 to 100 based on a topic's proportion to all searches on all topics".1 Use it to compare interest, such as "ssc cgl" against "ssc chsl", or to see when interest peaks before an exam, not to estimate how many buyers exist.



### 4. Search suggestions on Google and YouTube

Type the start of your topic into Google and YouTube and note what they suggest: "spoken english for interview", "spoken english in hindi", "ssc maths tricks in hindi". Google says its autocomplete "predictions reflect real searches that have been done on Google".2 The suggestions show you the words students use, which become your course title and page headings.



### 5. Ask five students the money question

Send your one-sentence offer to five students who fit it and ask: "Would you pay ₹999 for this?" You are not looking for encouragement. You are looking for the objection: "Is there a test?", "Will doubts be cleared?", "Is it in Hindi?". That objection is what your course, demo lesson or price must answer.






## Step 3: Outline and record a minimum course

A minimum course is the smallest complete course that fully delivers your one promise: a free demo lesson, 8 to 12 focused video lessons, PDF notes and a short test. It is small in scope, never unfinished in substance.



An illustrative minimum course for SSC CGL Percentage in Hindi.



### Outline before you record

Write the outline on one page, one idea per lesson. Exam courses follow the syllabus and end with a timed mock; skill courses follow practice: basics, drills, real use. Cut any lesson that does not move the student towards the promise.



### Record with what you have

Record on the phone or laptop you already own. A clip-on microphone is the one purchase worth making, because students forgive plain video far more easily than poor sound. Use a whiteboard, a writing tablet or slides. If being on camera is what stops you, our guide on how to teach online without showing your face shows voice-and-screen formats that sell just as well.



### Add notes, a test and one live session

A PDF of notes or a formula sheet, a short quiz after each part and a final mock make the course feel complete. One live doubt class a week, recorded into the course, answers the student's biggest worry: "What if I get stuck?"

The word that matters is complete: ten lessons that fully get a student through SSC Percentage questions are a real product; forty that stop halfway are not.

When educators set up an academy with us, the slowest step is rarely the technology. It is deciding what the first course is and recording the demo lesson. Give those two things a fixed deadline, such as two weeks.






## Step 4: How to price your first online course

Price your first course against the result it gives and the student's other options, not against the hours you spent recording. Then work backwards from your first ₹10,000 to see how many buyers you need.



Three illustrative routes to ₹10,000 in sales, before fees and taxes.



### Build a small price ladder



ProductIllustrative first priceIts job

PDF notes or formula pack₹99–₹299Turns a follower into a first-time buyer
Chapter-wise test series₹199–₹999Shows your teaching gets results
Recorded course₹499–₹2,999Your core product
Course with weekly live doubt classes₹1,499 and upFor students who want more of your time

Illustrative ranges, not market data. Your subject, exam and audience decide the right number.


A cheap first product exists to get a stranger to pay you once. After that, buying the full course is a much smaller step. Do not give the whole course away to "build an audience": give away one excellent demo lesson instead. For a full method, including when to raise the price, read how to price your online course in India.


Question educators ask



### Should my first course be free so people trust me?

Give away a sample, not the product. One strong free lesson builds trust. A free course mostly attracts people who will wait for the next free thing. Even a small payment makes students more likely to finish and ask doubts.







## Step 5: Build a course page that sells

A course page that sells answers six things in order: the promise, a free demo lesson, the price with one button, what is included, who teaches, and reviews with an FAQ. Put it on your own domain so you can share one link everywhere.



An illustrative course page on a sample domain.


- One clear promise at the top: exam or skill, outcome, language and time.

- A free demo lesson so the student can judge your teaching before paying.

- The price and one button. No "DM for fees". One button that leads to checkout.

- What is included: number of lessons, notes, tests, live classes, validity and the app.

- Who teaches: your real experience in plain words. Never promise ranks or selection.

- Reviews and an FAQ that answer refund, validity, language and device questions.


Most of your students will open the page on a phone, often from a WhatsApp link. Keep the top of the page short, make the button easy to tap, and test it on a budget Android phone. Our guide on how to create a landing page for an online course covers each part with examples.

A web address such as youracademy.in/ssc-maths-hindi looks like a real academy and stays yours if you change tools later. Every AllCoaching plan includes connecting your own domain, so the course page, checkout and your app all carry your name.






## Step 6: Take payments by UPI, with access on payment

Indian students expect to pay by UPI, so your checkout should accept UPI and cards, and open the course automatically once the payment succeeds. A QR code in a WhatsApp chat and a Google Drive link is not a checkout.

UPI is how India pays. NPCI data reported by Outlook Money shows UPI processed 24.07 billion transactions worth ₹29.37 lakh crore in September 2026 alone (checked October 2026).3 Asking students to do anything harder at checkout loses sales.



### Why WhatsApp QR and Drive links break

The manual setup breaks by the third buyer: you check screenshots, add people by hand and send Drive links that get forwarded. There is no record of who bought what, no way to remove access, and nothing that tells a stranger this is a real academy.

A proper checkout fixes all of that: the student pays by UPI or card, access opens on its own, and you get a record of every sale. Our guide on how to accept UPI payments for online courses explains gateways, KYC and charges.

On AllCoaching, UPI and card checkout is built into every plan, with automatic payouts through Razorpay. The student pays on your course page or in your app and starts learning straight away.

One note on records: course income is taxable income, and GST rules depend on your turnover and situation. Keep clean records from the first sale and read GST and income tax for online tutors in India, or ask your accountant.






## Step 7: Launch to your warm audience on WhatsApp, YouTube and Instagram

Your first buyers will almost always come from people who already know you: past students, WhatsApp groups, YouTube subscribers and Instagram followers. Plan a one-week launch for them before you spend anything on ads.



An illustrative launch week. Logos belong to their owners.



### Who is in your warm audience

List everyone who has seen you teach: former students, parents, your groups, subscribers, followers and colleagues. Even a few hundred people who trust you can be enough for 5 to 10 first buyers (illustrative). They are also mostly on their phones: TRAI reported 1,114.17 million internet subscribers in India at the end of June 2026, of whom 1,066.43 million were wireless (checked October 2026).4



### WhatsApp: conversation and reminders

Announce the offer and course link in your groups, send a reminder before the start date and reply to every question personally. For larger lists, see how educators use WhatsApp Channels for coaching.



### YouTube: proof and reach

Post the demo lesson with the course link in the description and pinned comment, and hold a short YouTube Live Q&A. If YouTube is your main channel, our guide to moving YouTube viewers into your own academy goes further.



### Instagram: trust in short form

Share short clips, a peek at the notes and doubts you answered, with the course link in your bio and stories.

YouTube and Instagram are where people meet you, WhatsApp is where you talk, and your course page is where they pay. Turn followers on rented platforms into a student list in your own academy that you can contact when batch 2 opens.


Question educators ask



### I have no followers. Who will buy my first course?

Start with people who have seen you teach: past students, parents, colleagues and local groups. Share one strong free lesson and the course link with them personally. If even that list is very small, spend a few weeks posting free lessons on YouTube or Instagram first, then launch.







## Step 8: After the first sale: reviews, word of mouth and batch 2

After your first sales, ask every happy student for a short review, help them tell friends, use their doubts to improve the course, and open the next batch on the same page. The first students are how you find the next ones.



The loop after the first sale. Concept diagram.


- Ask for reviews early. Two lines and a result ("cleared my doubts on Profit & Loss in a week") while it is fresh. Add them to the course page.

- Make word of mouth easy. Ask happy students to share the course link with one friend preparing for the same exam. Personal recommendations travel fast in exam groups.

- Use their doubts. The questions your first buyers ask are your next lessons, your FAQ and your next course.

- Open batch 2. Same page, new start date, better reviews. A dated batch gives students a reason to decide now.



"The first sale is not just revenue. It is proof that the promise was clear, the price was fair and a stranger trusted you enough to pay."

Amit Ratan, Founder & CEO, AllCoaching

Add paid ads after your course has sold to a warm audience, and start SEO early because it takes months to build. Ads can scale what already works; they rarely fix an offer nobody wanted.



### First paid ads on Facebook and Instagram

Once 5 to 10 people have bought, you know your offer and the buyers' questions, and a small Meta ads test makes sense: a reel that teaches something real, sent to the course page, with Meta Pixel tracking purchases. ## Glossary


Minimum course
The smallest complete course that fully delivers one promise, such as a demo lesson, 8 to 12 focused videos, PDF notes and a short test.
Demand validation
Checking that students want a course before recording it, using signals such as repeated comments, poll answers, search suggestions and students saying they would pay.
Warm audience
People who already know your teaching: past students, parents, WhatsApp groups, YouTube subscribers and Instagram followers.
Course page
The web page for one course that states the promise, shows a demo lesson, lists what is included and leads to checkout.
UPI checkout
A payment step where a student pays by UPI (or card) on your course page and gets access automatically when the payment succeeds.
Price ladder
A set of products at rising prices, such as a notes pack, a test series, a recorded course and a course with live doubt classes.
Platform fee
The percentage of each sale an academy platform keeps. On AllCoaching it is 10% on Starter, or 0% on Growth and Pro.

An online teaching platform for a spoken English trainer has to do three things that a general video tool does not — run small live batches where every learner actually speaks, store each learner's recordings so progress becomes visible, and hold enrolment, levels and fees in one place. That is the practical answer. But the reason those three requirements are the right ones, rather than the usual feature checklist, comes from a structural fact about this category that almost no guide states plainly: spoken English is the only major tutoring market in India with no examination attached to it.

Sit with how unusual that is. A Class 12 student gets marks. A NEET aspirant gets a mock rank every week. A CA student gets a result that is unambiguous and public. Every one of those teachers has an external authority that periodically tells the student, and the parent, whether the teaching is working. A spoken English trainer has nothing. There is no board, no rank, no certificate anyone respects, and no moment at which an outside party confirms that the learner is better than they were. IELTS exists but serves a different purpose and a different learner; for the vast majority of Indian spoken English students — the job seeker, the homemaker, the shopkeeper, the fresher facing placements — no test will ever be taken.

Across the educators onboarding on AllCoaching in 2026, spoken English trainers describe their problem in ways that sound unrelated to each other: "students leave after a few weeks", "people ask the price and disappear", "everyone teaches this, how do I stand out". Those are three symptoms of one cause. This guide follows that cause through to its consequences, because once you see it, the format, the pricing and the platform decisions all follow from it rather than from preference.





Key Takeaways — the entire post in six facts:


- Spoken English is the only major Indian tutoring category with no exam — no marks, no rank, no external validator. Every other problem in this business descends from that.

- Learners quit around week three because fluency improves too gradually to notice, enthusiasm fades, and nothing visible replaces it.

- A day-one baseline recording is the single highest-leverage habit — it is the only durable proof of progress the category permits, and it doubles as your best marketing.

- Batch size is arithmetic, not preference — 60 minutes across 20 learners is 3 minutes each at best, and in practice the quiet ones speak for zero.

- Sell a cohort, not a monthly fee — a fixed start and end creates commitment and a natural moment to collect before-and-after proof.

- On AllCoaching the studio starts at ₹6,999 a year — live batches, learner records, material selling and fee collection, no setup fee, a 10% platform fee only on what you sell on Starter or 0% commission on Growth and Pro.

"Nobody has ever walked out of a spoken English class saying the teaching was poor. They walk out saying 'I don't think it's working' — which is a completely different complaint, and the only one you can actually prevent."
